speechtext: The House proceeded to the consideration of Bill C-76, an Act to provide for emergency preparedness and to make related amendments to the National Defence Act, as reported (with an amendment) from a legislative committee.

speakeroldname: Hon. Perrin Beatty (Minister of National Defence) moved
speechtext: that the Bill be concurred in.
Motion agreed to.
that the Bill be read the third time and passed.

speakeroldname: Mr. Bud Bradley (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on June 26 of last year the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Beatty) tabled Bill C-76 in the House and announced that the federal Government had withdrawn the Emergency Planning Order of 1981 and was introducing new federal emergencies legislation to replace it.
As events continually show, emergencies do not wait for any timetable; they can happen at any time anywhere in Canada. With the adoption of Bill C-76, Parliament will be moving a step closer to a highly effective emergency planning and response system.
The Auditor General's annual report for the fiscal year ending March 1, 1987, included a special examination of emergency preparedness arrangements. He specifically recommended that consideration be given to providing statutory authority for federal emergency planning, and for the Government to declare a national emergency in peacetime. More explicitly, Mr. Dye said, "Co-ordination and the testing of specific national emergency plans between federal entities and between the federal Government and the provinces should be made the responsibility of a designated federal agency.
Emergency Preparedness Canada, the agency responsible for co-ordinating this response, has never had its role, responsibilities and mandate set out in an Act of Parliament; it has been acting under a series of ad hoc authorities that were not subject to parliamentary scrutiny.
This Bill will go a long way toward meeting the Auditor General's concerns. On behalf of the Minister responsible for emergency preparedness, I wish to thank Members of the legislative committee who reviewed this Bill carefully. It is a tribute to their understanding of the importance for the federal Government to be able to act swiftly and decisively in emergencies that they moved Bill C-76 forward so quickly. I am sure that the other place will see fit to deal with Bill C-76 as expeditiously.

Mr. Speaker, my remarks will be very brief and to the point. Bill C-76 is essentially a Bill that is administrative in nature to replace the Emergency Measures Organization. The Official Opposition has no difficulties with the Bill as it reports to the House. As we have indicated earlier, it simply establishes the rules under which provinces will be entitled to declare an emergency, and it utilizes all of the resources of the federal institutions to aid the provincial authorities in dealing with emergencies.
Frankly, Mr. Speaker, we have no difficulty with Bill C-76. 1 would imagine that the debate will lie in committee on Bill C-77 where there will be a clause-by-clause examination in the coming days and which will then report back to the House on Bill C-77.

Mr. Speaker, 1 must say that I breathed a sigh of relief this morning when the Government introduced its amendment.
The amendment was necessary because when the Bill was first introduced it sent a shudder through the country. As the House will recall, Clause 5(1) in part indicated the following:
The functions of Emergency Preparedness Canada with respect to the
development of civil emergency plans are ...
(f) to provide for the continuity of government during and after an emergency.
The Government was saying that if an emergency occurred, Emergency Preparedness Canada would become the Government of Canada. It would set aside our constitutional rights and our parliamentary rights. It would do away with the House of Commons and the other place-the whole institution of Parliament.

March 11, 1988
Borrowing Authority
I hope that it was simply a drafting oversight, but it sent a shudder throughout the country. I think the Government was about to set up what would essentially be a dictatorial panel to run Canada.
However, that has been clarified this morning, thank goodness, through the amendment with which we have already dealt.
Are you for or against it?

I hear my friend across the way from Ottawa- Carleton. He can bet that I am for it. We already have a Government which has lost some of its senses in terms of some of its powers, but to give it emergency powers into the future to do away with Parliament-
Nelson, that clause was their only hope, given the polls.

As my hon. colleague indicates, given the polls, perhaps it was their only hope for staying in government for some time beyond the next few months.
However, setting that aside, I do not want to sound flippant as it is a very serious piece of legislation. Having made those comments with regard to Bill C-76, I want to applaud the Government for having brought it forward.
As we know, the previous Government was going to deal with emergency situations through Privy Council Order 1305, which was a very worrisome piece of legislation. For example, it allowed for such ridiculous things as the planning of civilian internment camps. In other words, it would give the Government, with no accountability whatsoever, the right to set up civilian internment camps around the country, presumably to herd Canadian into during a state of emergency. The previous Liberal Government had no mandate from Parliament or legislative authority for such action. Parliament would have had no way to monitor what was going on even after the fact.
While Bill C-76 is a housekeeping Bill in many respects, it is certainly very welcome and long overdue when we consider what the Liberals had introduced for their so-called emergency preparedness.
While we are fortunate to live in a peaceful and relatively prosperous country, we tend sometimes to take these conditions for granted. However, we have had reminders in the past little while, such as the Edmonton tornado, the very serious Mississauga train derailment, and the ongoing discussions on the West Coast about a possible earthquake and the damage and chaos which would result from such an event. Obviously we must be prepared. We need emergency planning to guarantee help for those people stricken by a disaster and to ensure a rapid return to normal circumstances. This has really been put off for too long, which basically means that Canada and Canadians have been put at risk.
Thank goodness that Privy Council Order 1305 has now been put aside. Bill C-76 changes all this. The Minister of
National Defence (Mr. Beatty) will be responsible to Parliament for emergency planning. Essentially he will become the lead Minister during a crisis in the country. However, as a result of the Bill, parliamentarians will be able to scrutinize government activities and government spending in the area of emergency planning to ensure that the plans are appropriate, protect Canadians, and do not threaten the rights of Canadians.
One component of the Liberal initiative a few years ago under Privy Council Order 1305 concerned many of us who pride ourselves on being parliamentarians. I am referring to the opportunity to set up civilian internment camps. At that time questions were asked in the House about why the Government felt it was necessary to set up such camps and why it was necessary to have this particular power as a result of the Privy Council Order. It caused a lot of concern for Canadians who remembered their previous experiences in other countries when Governments had the right to set up internment camps for civilian populations.
Obviously the amendment is welcome because it supports the principle of constitutional government. The amendment itself indicates that we will establish arrangements for ensuring the continuity of constitutional government during an emergency. This is what we struggled to have included, and I thank the Government for seeing the wisdom in doing just that. It will ensure that emergency planning will aim to restore Parliament as soon as possible. I think it is a very appropriate measure.
Once the Bill has passed, Parliament will have told the Government to ensure that necessary measures are taken to protect Canadians in an emergency. As Canadians, people have a right to expect peace, order, and good government. While they have the right to expect peace and order, I guess Canadians are wondering whether in fact they have good government. In principle that is something we certainly want to see in place. When the situation is disturbed by some unforeseen disaster like the Edmonton tornado, Canadians expect their Government to be prepared to come to their assistance quickly or expeditiously. They expect their Government to have a great deal of tentative planning in place to provide for such an emergency, and Bill C-76 gives the Government the proper mandate from the Parliament of Canada to plan for such protection.
Motion agreed to, Bill read the third time and passed.

He said: Mr. Speaker, in my weakened condition today, I should like to make some very brief remarks on Bill C-109, an Act to provide borrowing authority.
First I should like to thank very much members of the House of Commons finance committee for the expeditious way in which they have dealt with the Bill. Certainly their cooperation will assist the Government in moving ahead with the process of an orderly debt management program in dealing with the substantial cash requirements of the Government of Canada.
As a Government we have fulfilled our responsibilities following the budget process as I outlined in the discussion paper some three years ago. We said that we wanted to have a Budget, the Main Estimates, and that thereafter we would present a borrowing authority Bill and look for speedy passage in order to allow us to proceed with our financial program.
Also the finance committee has fulfilled its responsibilities by dealing with the Bill expeditiously in committee as part of the budget debate. I thank Hon. Members. It is a good example of Members of Parliament from all Parties showing how Parliament can work in a very effective manner.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1988-89 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to begin by commenting briefly on the Minister's statement that the opposition Parties had co-operated in speedy passage of this Bill. We in the Official Opposition did this because the Government must be able to carry on its business in an orderly way. While we may not always agree with the way in which that business is carried on, the Government does have a mandate from the Canadian people and we respect that and have not delayed the Bill unusually. But I must point out that when the Minister was in opposition, his Party generally kept the borrowing authority in the House for weeks.
I must also remind the House that when the borrowing authority Bill was introduced a couple of weeks ago, it was introduced after the presentation of an insubstantial, empty Budget, which was replete with self-congratulation. In fact, one newspaper commentator wondered if the Minister might have slipped a disc patting himself on the back. This approval we were initially asked to give on faith because we had not even seen the Estimates.
I listed my misgivings in my speech at second reading and during the Budget debate. This morning I wish to reiterate just a few crucial points and raise others concerning the financial management of the Government.
Borrowing Authority
For this particular Bill, the Government asks for authority to borrow $25.3 billion after a Budget which was long on selfcongratulation and short on substance. The Government really is asking to borrow too much money when one considers that it has not kept its promises, a key one being that taxes would not be raised and the deficit would be lowered.
We initially said we would not pass this Bill until we saw the Estimates. Indeed, having seen the Estimates did not inspire any great confidence either. There were a number of items the Government announced which were not covered in the Estimates, and obviously later in the year there will be Supplementary Estimates. There is also some money on reserve which has not been defined and, again, there is a mystery about how this money will be spent.
I want to talk a bit about the federal sales tax. In the February 10 Budget, the Minister spoke of new rules concerning the manufacturers' sales tax. This is a tax which has been described by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) as a killer of jobs and is to be replaced sometime in the future by a new consumption sales tax. That date though is being put farther and farther back. Officials at the Department of Finance are now talking about a three to four year time frame for the new consumption sales tax, so that the increased use of the manufacturers' of sales tax, which was supposed to be an interim measure, will clearly be with us for some time. The Government is continuing to raise taxes, yet the public debt is not being reduced.
Here are some of the increases Canadians have experienced since 1984. There was an increase of 1 per cent in the sales tax in 1984, which brought $1 billion to the Government's Treasury. In 1986 there was a second increase of 1 per cent in the sales tax, bringing another $1 billion to the Government's Treasury. In 1986, we had a third increase of 1 per cent in sales tax, bringing in a further $1 billion. In 1985, we saw an increase of 2 cents a litre on gas, bringing in $930 million in revenue. In 1987, there was a second increase of 1 cent a litre on gas, bringing a further $450 million in revenue. In 1987, the equalization of sales tax on leaded and unleaded gasoline netted the Government $30 million. In 1985, we had the extension of sales tax on candy, soft drinks and pet food, netting the Government $400 million. In 1987, the extension of sales tax on snack foods brought the Government $60 million. In 1985, we saw the first increase in cigarette and tobacco taxes, amounting to $320 million in revenue to the Government.
In 1986, there was a second increase in tobacco and alcohol taxes, netting $150 million to the Government this time. In 1987, we had a third increase of 4 per cent in tobacco taxes, amounting to $70 million. In 1985, we saw the elimination of the Registered Home Ownership Savings Program, which captured for the Government $105 million in revenue. In 1986, there was the deindexation of the personal income tax system, which brought the Government $635 million. The elimination of the federal tax reduction in 1986 captured $650 million. Changes to marital exemptions in 1986 brought in $20 million.

March 11, 1988
Borrowing Authority
The general 3 per cent surtax in 1986 netted $1,200 million, and that surtax is still there.
Many of the measures which I have described go on from year to year silently. They are no longer shown specifically in Budgets because they have been built into the system. While this Government raises and raises taxes, the public debt is not being reduced. We have also seen some creative accounting to indicate that the debt is lower than it is. I spoke on this point before and it has been commented on by external, more objective authorities perhaps, such as the Bank of Montreal and in Peat Marwick's tax letter.
Then we come to the question of fiscal transfers to the provinces. Not long after this Government came to power, it said a cap would be put on the growth of fiscal transfers to the Government. The Government did not like calling this a cut. It said it was limiting growth. That was the statement in Canada. However, in February, 1986, in a special glossy publication called The Canadian Budget in Perspective, which was distributed to our embassies overseas, the Government stated:
The rate of increase of federal transfers to provincial Governmehts for
health care and post-secondary education has been reduced.
This information was not in the 1986 Budget Speech, but the provinces are certainly aware of it and are feeling the effects now.
The Government has certainly made some absolutely enormous tax grabs. The question is, can the taxpayers be assured that the Government is practising sound financial management? Unfortunately, we cannot assure them of that. The amount required to finance the national debt has risen steadily since this Government came to power. In this, our sixth year of recovery after the recession, we are not likely to see the rapid growth that we experienced in pre-recession years. That is why the Government must be particularly responsible when managing its expenditures and managing the national debt.
In the past, Canada and other western democracies relied on increased economic growth to redress social disparities. We are not likely to see again the kind of very rapid growth that was experienced some years ago, but we still want to maintain our social programs and equality of opportunity in the workforce and in the educational system. Canadians should not have to come from wealthy families in order to obtain post-secondary education and equip themselves for satisfying careers. We also need to be aware of regional disparities, but all these services must be delivered effectively, efficiently and economically.
My Party and I have always regarded as an essential plank of Liberalism the goal of social betterment. Therefore, in consideration of future generations of Canadians and in consideration of having options to develop programs that make for real equality of opportunity, we must not compromise our future by anything less than prudent financial management.
Let us look at some of the frivolous expenses we have seen the Government approve. We have seen one plane following another when the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) travels. We have seen a plane to carry video equipment. We have seen extraordinarily increased travel expenses.

In these times-yes, the Conservative Member says, "nonsense". I absolutely agree with him. Indeed, it is nonsense to spend money frivolously when there are still Canadians who are living in poverty, there are still children who are living in poverty and who will not be able to achieve their full potential.
With those remarks, I would exhort the Government to make some real attempt to manage better, to spend money in the best interests of Canadians, to develop sound public policies, to limit the frivolous expenses and to stop this policy of tax more and spend more.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1988-89 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am less than happy to have the chance to make some remarks today about this borrowing Bill. I know that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) is here, so I will say the good thing I have to say right off the top.
For many years, while the Liberals were in government, borrowing authority Bills would trickle in throughout the year. We would be asked to approve $5 billion here, $10 billion there and $6 billion there. This was done to try to give the impression that the Liberals were not borrowing very much. Estimates and Budgets were brought in at all times of the year in an attempt to destabilize the management of the country's finances.
At that time, we advocated that the Budget should be brought in at a particular time each year and that the borrowing requirements ought to be identified and the Estimates and tax expenditures provided all in one fell swoop. By and large, the Government is doing that. That is the good news, and I think we have made some progress in enabling parliamentarians to understand the nation's financial arrangements.
Today the Government is asking us to approve the borrowing of $25.3 billion. I do not think that we need to borrow $25.3 billion. I think it is unfortunate that so much of this is going to servicing a debt that keeps going up and up. While the deficit has stabilized somewhat, it is still too large.
I cannot for the life of me understand why the Minister of Finance does not rise later today, perhaps close to midday, to announce that he is concerned about the high interest rates that went up this week, as a matter of fact. They marginally increased again. There is a tremendous gap that exists between Canadian short-term interest rates and short-term interest rates in the United States.
If the Minister of Finance were to say that he was concerned about the deficit and the increasing debt and that one of the ways to deal with that quickly and efficiently would be to
March 11, 1988

reduce interest rates so that the cost of servicing the debt is reduced, that one decision could start reducing the debt of Canada by billions of dollars. I would hope that we would see some action on that front taken by the Minister of Finance shortly. That is to say nothing of the benefits that would accrue to many Canadians if there were to be another drop in the interest rates of 1 per cent or 2 per cent.
I was hoping that the Minister of Finance would use the opportunity today to explain what the $2.5-billion slush fund will be used for. In the Estimates, there is a very clear listing of $2.5 billion, with no indication of what government programs will be used for. Some of us call it a pre-election slush fund which gives the Government the ability to dish out a few million dollars here, a few million dollars there, for this project and that project, to try to enhance the Government's image. As the Gallup poll reminded us yesterday, that image still needs enhancing. At 28 per cent, the Government still has a long way to go.
Quite frankly, I am astounded by that figure, considering that the Government has 208 Members of Parliament going across the country selling their policies. They have unlimited government expenses to sell their policies, and still the people of Canada are able to see through all of this. They know that the Government does not represent the ordinary Canadian but represents instead a very select, small group of Canadians, a very influential, powerful, wealthy minority. That minority is represented well, but ordinary Canadian citizens must look to other Parties, and I suspect that they will probably look to the New Democratic Party the next time they go to the polls.
My hon. friend from Trinity started to outline the long list of silly expenditures of this Government. If we are interested ill reducing government spending, we could reduce interest rates, the most obvious initiative. The second most obvious initiative would be to eliminate the slush fund. A thifd initiative would be to do away with the silly spending the Government has done. The Hon. Member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson) indicated that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) feels that he has to lug an extra plane along filled with movie and video equipment in order to catch the few good things he does across Canada, presumably for election purposes. There is a long list of other such expenditures.
Some of the most powerful people in Canada built the West Edmonton Mall, and they came to the Government and asked for $5 million. The Minister of Finance said: "Right on, here is $5 million," wrote out a cheque and gave it to them. They did not need $5 million to build the West Edmonton Mall. Again, this is one of the richest families in Canada, one of the most influential business families, and the Government wrote them out a cheque for $5 million. Quite frankly, time does not permit me to go through the long list of peculiar government expenditures.
I noticed with interest today that the unemployment rates in parts of Canada have increased. Let me talk about the constituency that I represent. Back in September of 1984 when
Borrowing Authority
the present Government was elected, the unemployment rate in Kamloops-Shuswap was 16.3 per cent. This morning, the unemployment rate is at 20.9 per cent. In other words-

That is indicative as well of constituencies surrounding Kamloops-Shuswap including the Kootenays area and the northern part of British Columbia. I could list constituencies right across the country.
We appreciate that prosperity has returned to pockets in Ontario. However, that prosperity does not exist in other parts of Canada. In fact, since the Progressive Conservative Government took office, the unemployment statistics indicate that in Kamloops-Shuswap, there has been an increase in unemployment of over 4 per cent. In other words, when the question is put to people in the regions: Is your life better today than it was in September of 1984? The answer is clear: Absolutely not.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1988-89 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Absolutely yes.

speechtext:
If you ask that question in a select few centres in Ontario, the answer is yes. Not all of Ontario. With the big closure of Massey, thousands of people are going to be out of work. Thousands of other people who depend upon that industry will be out of work. Look at northern Ontario, northern Quebec, Atlantic Canada, the North, the West, including British Columbia. As you well know, the situation for most Canadians living in the regions is not better than it was back in September of 1984. That is the proof of the pudding. That is why I am puzzled that the Minister of Finance did not stand in his place today and say: We recognize this reality. We recognize that the economic prosperity we find in parts of Ontario does not exist in the regions. We, as a compassionate, concerned, caring Government, are going to take steps to overcome that. Yet, no, the Minister was mute on this issue.
When you add up the regional development expenditures of the Government you see there have been cuts in the percentage of money going to the regions. When you look at the funding of the western diversification fund you find there has been a reduction in relative terms in funds set aside for regional economic expansion in western Canada.
This is a very serious issue and there are so many initiatives the Government could take to assist the regions. I just want to go through two or three to help the Minister of Finance if he is looking for initiatives the Government can take to assist people in the regions. Let me suggest a few that would apply to one part of British Columbia.
There is a major dependency on the forest resource in that province. The resource needs to be improved. It needs to be nurtured, supported, developed, husbanded. The forest requires

March 11, 1988
Borrowing Authority
thinning programs, spacing programs, fertilizing programs, disease and pest control programs, road building, research and development. Provincial foresters say there are thousands and thousands of jobs that need to be done to husband that resource; not could be done, but must be done if we are going to maintain the industry as we know it today, let alone expand it.
What about agriculture? When you look at the farms across the country you recognize that we are rapidly approaching what for many farmers can only be described as a debt crisis. The cost of growing food overshadows the revenue. Our farmers are in a very serious situation these days. What is the Government doing about it? Is it providing long-term low interest loans to farmers? No. Do the interest rates of the Farm Credit Corporation make sense for the farm community? No. It is time that the Minister of Finance and his colleagues recognized that for the farm sector to survive, and it is quite capable of doing so given its human and natural resources, it has to have money at acceptable interest rates. That means around the 6 per cent level. That can be done. Other countries do it. Yet the Government of Canada refuses to take this step.
What about all of the other programs that could be put in place? For example, a decent child care program. We learned just the other day that over 60 per cent of the women of this country are in the workforce, yet decent child care facilities are just not in place. It disappoints me to have to say that my province is one of the worst offenders. There are tens of thousands of young children in inappropriate child care facilities because there are no alternatives. Their parents have to work to maintain the family. Yet there are very few adequate child care facilities in that province.
Why does the federal Government not take some steps to provide some leadership in child care so those hundreds of thousands of young children in inadequate child care facilities every day are properly cared for? One spin-off would be job creation. Another would be the peace of mind for the parents. Flere is an initiative which must be taken in a progressive country in the 1980s.
I wanted the Minister of Finance to indicate today that he had rethought his tax reform program. I think most Canadian families now know that since the Conservative Government took office in September of 1984, the average family, regardless of tax reform, will be paying at least $1,000 more in federal taxes. That means $1,000 out of the pockets and purses of every Canadian family. That money is just taken to Ottawa. It does not circulate in the Chicoutimis and Red Deers and Thunder Bays. The money should be distributed to where it can be used most appropriately and effectively and that is in the hands of Canadians. Stop gouging. Stop prying every cent out of families.
If you ask the question: How are these expenditures going to be made up? I will tell you how. Why, if we have a progressive country, would we permit a situation where, in spite of tax
reform, 60,000 profitable corporations will still be in a position to pay not a single penny in income tax? The Americans do not tolerate that. The U.S. looked around and saw that in 1986 there were hundreds of thousands of firms not paying one penny in income tax in spite of their profits. Those profits might be $100 million or $200 million or $300 million, yet they are still not paying a penny in federal taxes. Congress said that was not right, that was unfair, unjust and discriminatory. When those profitable corporations pay nothing, the average working person has to pay more than he or she should be paying.
Our Government does not take that attitude. I could not believe the Minister of Finance when he walked in a little while back and said we are going to introduce tax reform, and then opened up his book to explain what it was all about. He said we are still going to allow 60,000 profitable corporations to escape paying taxes. These are not your beauty salons or welding shops on the corner. They include Power Corporation, Argus Corporation, Cadillac-Fairview, the Royal Bank of Canada, Shell Oil, General Motors. In some years they do not pay a single penny in income tax. Can you imagine a tax system in the 1980s that allows a teller working for the Royal Bank or the Bank of Montreal to pay more income tax in some years than the entire Royal Bank or Bank of Montreal? Yet that is what our tax system permits and will continue to permit.

Why should we tolerate it for a minute?
When the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) comes before Parliament, as he has done today, and asks for the authority to borrow $25.3 billion, I think it is only right for us to ask why we do not have an effective and fair tax system which collects billions of dollars more each year. These are questions that Canadians are asking. These are questions which ought to be answered if the Minister of Finance believes that what he is doing is appropriate, right, fair, and honest.
Since the Minister refuses to answer these questions I can only assume that the Government is trying to play a smoke and
March 11, 1988

mirrors game, trying to pull the wool over the eyes of Canadians. However, I do not think the Government can do it. I think Canadians realize that our tax system is unjust, unfair, discriminatory and biased, that it favours large corporations over small businesses and upper-income influential Canadians over the ordinary Canadian working man and woman.
These are the realities. I think that the Minister of Finance or other members of the Cabinet should stand today in this debate to explain to the people of Canada why the Government continues to keep this unjust system in place at the same time as he asks permission to borrow more than $25 billion.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with a certain sense of regret that I participate in this debate. Canadians are indicating to the Government in a variety of ways, particularly through polls, that they are very preoccupied with the state of the environment. Yet the Government is not paying attention to that public preoccupation and has come forward in its budgetary provisions for this fiscal year with a budget for Environment Canada which increases the monetary allocation to that Department by 3.6 per cent. To put that in context, the over-all increase in government spending this year is 8 per cent. Inflation is 4.5 per cent. Therefore, in its 1988-89 budget, Environment Canada loses twice, first in relation to the over-all increase of the Government and, second, with an increase which is below the rate of inflation.
Once again, since 1984 the Department of the Environment is not able, with the money it is receiving from the Minister of Finance and Treasury Board, to keep up with inflation, let alone make any further expansions or launching the programs which need to be launched in light of the environmental situation which is emerging, particularly in water and air, which demands a strong federal presence and strong initiative through federal programs.
While Environment Canada is receiving only a 3.6 per cent increase to its budget this year, other Departments of the Government are doing extremely well. For example, the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources has increased its budget by 30 per cent, the Department of Agriculture by 24 per cent, the Department of Transport by 7.5 per cent, National Defence by 8.3 per cent, the Department of Communications by 11 per cent, the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development by 11.5 per cent, the Department of Finance by 13.5 per cent, and the Department of Fisheries and Oceans by 23 per cent.
If you compare the budget of Environment Canada in 1984 with the budget of Environment Canada today you will find that in relation to inflation it is weaker by no less than 17 per cent. Environment Canada has lost 17 per cent of its purchasing power between 1984 and 1988. As a result of this weakening of purchasing power, 336 positions have been lost over these four years. Scientists, technicians, and support people had to be dismissed over the course of these years as a result of this weakening of the Department's role.
While this is going on, the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) has come forward in the House and elsewhere and made strong statements about the Government's commitment to the environment. I regret to say that that strong commitment is, unfortunately, not backed up by facts. When you look at the figures and the budgetary performance, you discover with dismay that those words are hollow.
Two days ago there was in the Toronto Star a letter by the Minister of the Environment rushing to his own defence after two non-governmental groups pointed out that Environment Canada was getting a percentage increase well below the average increase of all other Departments. The Minister wrote a lengthy letter in defence of his actions. He states, first, that the increase for Environment Canada is 3.6 per cent. That is accurate and it is one of the reasons that I am pointing out to the Government that the Department, with inflation ranging between 4 and 4.5 per cent, is losing ground in terms of its purchasing power.
Second, in order to enhance the impact of his letter, the Minister of the Environment went on to say that there is $150 million in the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion in an attempt to create the impression that that money is available to that Department to enhance environmental programs.
Shall we call it eleven o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

Mr. Speaker, there is celebration in British Columbia and across Canada. Wolves are not to be shot from aircraft by government biologists because, in the opinion of the British Columbia Supreme Court, doing so violates the Government's own hunting laws. It is a victory for wildlife and a defeat for the contention of the Government of British Columbia that wolves should be exterminated to ensure sufficient numbers of elk, caribou, moose and stone sheep for commercial hunting.
Since 1982 the Government has killed about 1,000 wolves in an attempt to increase the numbers of those trophy animals that attract hunters from around the world.
This ruling is a victory in recognition that wildlife should no longer be the objective of reckless exploitation. The message is that wildlife has a greater value than the economic value we

March 11, 1988
assign and that each species plays an important role in the balance of nature.
Those who want to kill elk, caribou, moose and stone sheep for entertainment and relaxation, or for the sake of a stuffed trophy on their walls, are invited to find another hobby. They could trade their high powered rifles for a pair of cross country skis.

Mr. Speaker, every port city has its special memories and the Port of Halifax is no exception. This week and throughout 1988 attention will be focused on Pier 21 and its 60 years of history as Canada's gateway.
From 1928 to the 1970s, Pier 21 was the portal through which 1.25 million persons immigrated to become new Canadians. Equally important was the return to Canada of
400,000	soldiers from the strife of World War II, and some were later to be joined by their war brides.
These families are today represented in virtually every Canadian community, including Parliament. But Halifax Harbour and Pier 21 provided their first view of Canada.
Our ocean ports are no longer the entrance way to Canada for those seeking a new life and new opportunities, but we should recognize the role played by our immigration facilities and the officials and volunteers who served in them as these events pass into Canadian history.

Mr. Speaker, in celebrating International Women's Week, I take great pride in honouring the efforts of Canadian aboriginal women who are working for justice and equality. Unfortunately, while women in general have all too often suffered discrimination, aboriginal women have been hit even harder. These are women who are part of Canada's first nations, who have helped maintain cultural traditions and deserve our recognition.
First, let us honour those who worked tirelessly for legislation, which was eventually brought in in 1985, which brings the Indian Act in line with the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, and restores official recognition and federal services to thousands of native women and their children who lost their status by marrying non-status Indians.
We honour the women of the Tobique Band of New Brunswick, who marched in Ottawa in the late 1970s; Sandra Lovelace, who went to the United Nations on behalf of native women who had lost their status through marriage; Mary Two-Axe Early, who has been largely credited with the resulting change to the Indian Act in 1985; from the Yukon, Margaret Joe, the first aboriginal woman cabinet minister in Canada.
We honour also Mary Simon, president of the Ottawa based Inuit Circumpolar Conference; Maria Campbell, Metis author of Half Breed; Rosemarie Kuptana, president of the Inuit Broadcasting Corporation; Roberta Jamieson, a Mohawk lawyer and Indian Commissioner of Ontario; and Rhoda Innukshuk, president of the Inuit Tapirisat of Canada. We applaud the fine work of these women.

Mr. Speaker, Canada has shown consistency, has now demonstrated consistency by speaking out against human rights violations wherever they occur in whatever hemisphere, throughout the world.
Honest dialogue among friends and nations is seldom easy. Honest dialogue between friends can indeed be most difficult. While peace and security of all people, especially the people of Israel, is uppermost in the minds of Canadians, so, too, is our abhorrence of human rights violations by whomever, wherever.
I believe the Canadian position is now very clear. Canada cannot be loyal to friends in all things, if they cannot be true in all things to themselves.
To speak in this day and age of occupation-occupied land and occupied people-is a contradiction to the fundamental rights and freedoms which all people should be able to enjoy.
We would hope that we will now see some positive change to the attitudes and events of recent months in Palestine which have caused such dismay and anguish with all friends of Israel.

subtopic: REQUEST TO LOWER FARES TO YOUTH
REQUEST TO LOWER FARES TO YOUTH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a number of young people have been complaining that VIA Rail
March 11, 1988

is acting just like the Tory Government. Indeed, like the Government, this corporation is laughing at them. With or without the complicity of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie), it wanted to show its magnanimity towards young Canadians.
For some time, VIA Rail has been offering to young people, a 30 per cent discount on all normal rates on every day of the week. Is it an excessive reduction? No, Mr. Speaker, because such discount does not apply on Fridays and Sundays from noon to 6 p.m.! Now considering their status as student, it is precisely the two periods of the week when students can really travel by train. One could argue that such restriction ends at 6 p.m. and that students can travel by train later. But no, VIA Rail has anticipated such a move. There is no departure after 6 p.m. for the main places of destination where students are bound.
This is entirely unacceptable. Either VIA Rail shows that it really wants to help young people and offers an unrestricted discount or it continues to look ridiculous.
Who within the Tory Government will assume his responsibilities and solve that problem for young people? Since I have no confidence in the Minister of State (Youth) (Mr. Charest), I am directing my comment to the Minister of Transport.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Hees) announced this week that the federal and Ontario Governments will negotiate the transfer of the Rideau Veterans Home in Ottawa to the Perley Hospital and will open up 50 new chronic care-beds in a new jointly funded state of the art 450-bed geriatric facility to be built on the present National Defence Medical Centre Rideau Veterans Home site.
At present, 142 veterans are cared for at the Rideau Veterans Home and 50 veterans are in the care of the National Defence Medical Centre. In the new geriatric complex, 250 beds will become available for veterans. These additional beds will be a blessing for veterans who are waiting to get into the Rideau Veterans Home.
Furthermore, combining the Rideau Veterans Home and the National Defence Medical Centre would provide improved care for all veterans.
I am pleased that the federal Government will be working with the Ontario Government to bring about more and enhanced chronic care for both veterans and patients in a new geriatric facility. This is the work of a caring Government.

Mr. Speaker, Canadian women across the country celebrated last March 8 International Women's Day by staging numerous activities throughout the week. They celebrated victories won in the last decades and reviewed the work that remains to be done. We all know, Mr. Speaker, that the present Government did not keep the electoral promises it made to women. Its attitude on issues regarding the status of women was obvious this week.

On Tuesday, International Women's Day, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) was invited to take part in a panel discussion on the trade deal. He was unable to attend. Not one Conservative Member of Parliament could be found to address the concerns of the women of Ontario.
On Wednesday, a forum on women in federal politics was co-sponsored by the International Women's Week Committee, the National Action Committee on the Status of Women, and Canadian Women for Political Responsibility. Once more, the Conservatives could not find one Member to attend.
These absences call into question the Conservative Government's commitment to women despite the admirable promises we have heard in the House this week.

Mr. Speaker, the Progressive Conservative Party campaigned in the summer of 1984 on jobs, jobs, jobs.
In keeping with that theme, I am pleased to note the creation of a further 57,000 jobs in February of which 42,000 went to women. Some 515,000 jobs have been created in the past 12 months and the cumulative totals since this Government took office is 1.213 million. Furthermore, over 85 per cent of those jobs are full time, and over 50 per cent of them have gone to women.
Today there are 1.213 million more Canadians working than just three and one-half years ago. The unemployment rate, at 7.8 per cent, is at its lowest since August, 1981. In every province in this country the unemployment rate is lower than it was in September, 1984.
I congratulate the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) for their responsible approach to deficit reduction which has created an environment in which the initiative, entrepreneurship and energy of

March 11, 1988
Canadians has been able to manifest itself in this outstanding record of job creation.

Mr. Speaker, Quebecers mourn the loss of the most charming little boy, who was a ray of hope, who fought for his life, who built up courage and was confident in the future. That little boy was Charles Bruneau who appeared in advertisements for LEU-CAN. He suffered from leukemia, and right to the end, to the last minute, he was courageous and full of hope.

subtopic: REPRESENTATION OF WOMEN IN THE SCIENCES
REPRESENTATION OF WOMEN IN THE SCIENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Women in Scholarship, Engineering, Science and Technology, WISEST, is a committee made up of scientists, engineers, scholars, educators and students from the University of Alberta, the Alberta Government and the private sector. Its mandate is to increase the representation of women in all fields of scholarship, particularly in the areas of the sciences, engineering and technology, where women are very much under-represented in decision-making roles.
One initiative which WISEST has developed to increase the number of women in these fields is a program for Grade 11 high school students who spend six weeks during the summer working in established research groups at the University of Alberta. Between 15 and 25 students are accepted each summer. The program also includes small numbers of male students working in home economics and nursing. WISEST believes this program is unique in Canada. With Alberta's unemployment down 31 per cent since September 1984, such programs may be especially helpful in meeting specialized labour demands in the coming years.

Mr. Speaker, in October, 1970 the Pierre Trudeau Government was proclaiming a state of emergency and imposing war measures. Hundreds of people were arrested during the night, jailed and released without being charged with anything. Cities like Montreal and Ottawa were under siege. All freedoms were abolished. Today, notes taken by a former Minister, Mr. Donald Jamieson, show that there was no evidence of an insurrection.

The then Minister of Justice, now the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Turner), said that someday the Canadian people should know the facts about the imposition of the War Measures Act. EFFECT OF SALES TAX ON LONG DISTANCE TELEPHONE CALLS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last June the Government announced a 10 per cent tax on long distance telephone calls. That tax discriminates against rural
March 11, 1988

residents. If one lives in the country or a small town, one's business, school, and personal contacts are likely to be in another telephone exchange. This means that the taxes become an extra burden for businesses and citizens in rural areas, an extra burden carried not because of the use of the facility but because of where they live or carry on their business or, even in some cases, where they send their children to school.
It is time the Government corrected its mistake which discriminates against rural Canada.

Mr. Speaker, once again I rise to encourage the Government to show strong national leadership on a very sensitive and important social issue affecting families today, the issue of abortion. During the hearings held last year, the Committee on child care, of which I was a Member, was told of the need for support of the Canadian family.
I would hope that our society has, or will have, sufficient support mechanisms in place so that if a woman has a so-called "unwanted" pregnancy, counselling, support and constructive help for her and her unborn child will be easily accessible. She must realize that there is an alternative to abortion.
I have received approximately 1,800 letters from my constituents to date who feel that Parliament must recognize the unborn child and his or her right to life from the moment of conception. I would strongly urge that any legislation or proposed motion on this matter should be framed from the basis of the value of life. For the sake of the Canadian family, present and future, we must act strongly and with conviction.

subsubtopic: SUPERMAILBOXES-EFFECT ON TAX ASSESSMENTS- GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. It has to do with his famous supermailboxes. The Minister knows that the Ontario Municipal Board ruled a 5 per cent reduction in property taxes for some individuals. The Ontario Ministry of Revenue has stated that it will abide by that decision. It also stated that an additional 20 home owners who appealed their 1987 property tax assessments before this year's deadline, and who had those community boxes in front of or beside their homes, will qualify for this 5 per cent reduction.
I would like to ask the Minister who is responsible for protecting and promoting consumers' interests, if he will now inform the House as to what he is going to do about this nuisance caused by those so-called supermailboxes?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: SUPERMAILBOXES-EFFECT ON TAX ASSESSMENTS- GOVERNMENT POLICY

Mr. Speaker, prior to undertaking this program and fulfilling the policy which was laid down as long ago as 1974, the Post Office undertook test studies and had independent appraisers look at what effect those supermailboxes would have on the communities and on property values.
There was an independent appraisal done which stated that "Based on surveys undertaken in the three communities within York division, Streetsville, Oakville, and Markham, we find no evidence that the Canada Post superbox has any effect on value of neighbouring residential properties". That was stated by an independent appraiser.
Why the Ontario Municipal Board would reach the conclusion that it did, less than 48 hours after the supermailbox was in fact put into use, is something for the Government of Ontario to work out, and if it has reached its decision, it is entitled to do that.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary is to the same Minister. This Minister is abdicating his responsibilities for consumers in this country. He knows full well that an Ontario Municipal Board now supported by the Ministry of Revenue in the Government of Ontario has stated very clearly that his now famous super-duper mailboxes are a nuisance.
The Minister has a choice. He can either scrap this particular program, which is just absolutely ridiculous for Canadians, or he can compensate those individuals, particularly the municipalities that will lose revenue as a result.
Is the Minister going to accept his responsibilities and act on behalf of consumers as opposed to the corporate interests continuously?

Affairs): The Ontario Municipal Board reached a decision about two home owners and one location. That is all. Why that was extrapolated to include everybody else is a question that the Government of Ontario will have to answer.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. The Minister of Finance will be aware that the Conference Board of Canada which recently analyzed the Canada-U.S. trade deal released a report yesterday. Either to have taxes increased substantially, or to have a significant increase in the deficit.
Will the Minister of Finance indicate to the House and to the people of Canada which one of those options the Government plans to pursue?

Mr. Speaker, neither. The Hon. Member should refer to the budget papers that I put out with the last Budget which indicate that a 1 per cent increase in the economic growth in Canada will lead to $1.1 billion worth of increased revenues in the first year, and increasing after that. If that is transposed into what we expect is a 2.0 to 2.5 per cent increase in economic growth, it can be seen that that will be greater than the amount of revenues that would be lost as a result of the tariff reduction.
Also, Mr. Speaker, I think that the Hon. Member ignores the fact that we have a very strong economy, and a growing economy. In his earlier comments he ignored the fact that there was a .3 per cent reduction in the unemployment rate in February to 7.8 per cent, which is the lowest level since 1981.

Hear, hear!

Oral Questions

The increase in jobs created, as we now have over 1.2 million jobs created since September, 1984, together with other news of a 17 per cent increase in investment intentions, a very strong period of economic growth last year with the highest level of growth in the fourth quarter, indicate that we are going into 1988 in the strong period; all of those things together say that we have a very strong economy, an economy that is responding well to the economic policies of the Government of Canada. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I remind the Minister of Finance that in a number of areas of British Columbia the unemployment rates have increased from September, 1984 by four or five percentage points. It is higher than the national average, but that represents 138,000 jobs created and a drop in unemployment of 54,000 people. The economic policies of the Government of Canada are working in British Columbia as well as in other parts of Canada.
The Hon. Member is specifically asking how we will finance the drop in tariffs. I have indicated that because of the growth in the economy over and above what would be expected from the growth that is there now, which I indicated is very strong, additional revenues will be generated that are far more than what is necessary to cover the loss in tariff revenue.
What the Hon. Member is saying, that we have to use stage two tax reform to do this, demonstrates that he is out to lunch. He does not understand what he is talking about when he draws those conclusions.

Mr. Speaker, the Conference Board study is not the only one which has suggested that the Minister's projections are rosy and that economic growth in coming years will not be large enough to do all the things the Minister is anticipating. For instance, the Minister talks about increased employment, yet we know that we need 3
March 11, 1988

per cent growth just to stand still in terms of employment creation.
That is what we have been having.

Somebody says that that is what we have, but the Minister is saying that it is about to increase and that we will have a tremendous increase in employment.
Since the Conference Board study is not the only one which points out that there will be limits to growth, how in fact does the Minister intend to extract this $2.9 billion from Canadians whom he has already taxed almost beyond endurance?

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member is attacking my projections. I will go back to November, 1984 and compare my projections with those of other Members of the House of Commons. I remind her that her Leader said in November, 1984 and in May, 1985 that the policies of this Government would cost us 50,000 or 100,000 jobs. I believe that was the figure he used at that time. We have a strong economy. I have said that this year the economy will increase by 2.8 per cent. Some of the economists are coming out today and saying, as a result of the unemployment rate drop announced this morning, plus the investment intention increase of 17 per cent for this year, plus the strength in the fourth quarter last year which no one had anticipated, that my figures are low. They are saying that there will be a 3 per cent increase in growth this year.

Mr. Speaker, it is my duty and honour to present a petition from many residents of Canada on the subject of the Government's legislation in Bill C-55 which these citizens believe threatens Canada's traditional commitment to the assistance of refugees.
They point out that refugees reaching our border will be turned away without having their claims heard on the merits. They point out that the standing committee of Parliament did propose a procedure for refugees which would have been both quick and fair and which has received the support of all the public groups in Canada which have commented on it, including the churches and the Bar Association.

They ask Parliament to ensure that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) will end all the low-level flight training at Goose Bay Canadian Forces Base and cease negotiations with NATO for the establishment of a larger base there.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in resuming my intervention in this debate I would like to bring to your attention the fact that the Department of the Environment is being treated as the Cinderella of Departments of the Government. The amount being allocated to this Department this year, in terms of percentage, is less than half of the percentage increase of the over-all Budget for the fiscal year 1988-89.
As though this were not bad enough, upon considering what has happened to that Department since 1984 you find that the loss of purchasing power of the Department of the Environment as a result of inflation is in the range of 17 per cent. Every pensioner in this country and everyone who lives on a fixed income knows what it means to lose ground to inflation.
Borrowing Authority
This is exactly what is happening to the Department of the Environment despite the fact that in poll after poll Canadians are indicating that the condition of the environment is an issue to which they attribute one of the highest priorities.
As a result of this reduction of 17 per cent in purchasing power, the Department of the Environment has lost 336 scientists, technicians, and support people. How can this Department perform the role of vigilance, protection, advocacy and protection of the environment when it is not only not holding its own with regard to inflation but is, year after year, losing ground? That escapes the ability to understand of Members on this side of the House.
What is worse is the rhetoric of the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) who is trying to convince Canadians to the contrary, as is proven by the letter he wrote to the Toronto Star to which I made reference earlier in this debate. In a desperate attempt to create an impression that things are fine with regard to the budget of that Department, the Minister made reference to $106 million for the establishment of South Moresby over the next 10 years. That is a good development, but it has nothing to do with the capacity of the Environment Department to function this year.
In another desperate attempt to create a smoke and mirrors effect he mentions a $150 million allocation to the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion. That $150 million is in 1982 dollars and there is a very good reason for that. It has been ear-marked since 1982 to be made available to non-ferrous smelters when they proceed with the modernization of those plants in order to introduce anti-pollution equipment. It is a situation in which the Minister is invoking figures from other Departments to shore up the abysmal picture that is emerging for Environment Canada.
While I welcome a substantial increase, such as those for Agriculture and other Departments, it hurts to see this Department being treated like Cinderella, with an increase of 3.6 per cent in this year. At the same time, we must listen to the rhetoric of the Government and the Minister of the Environment, who claims the contrary. Not only does it hurt, it is offensive and disregards the priorities which Canadians want the Government to give to the environment.
We are on the eve of another summit in Washington next month between the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and President Reagan, where the question of acid rain will be raised again. The summit in Quebec City took place in 1985. It was an expensive event at which the Prime Minister displayed his skills as a tenor. I do not know whether that was good enough to convince President Reagan that Canadians mean business about the matter of transboundary pollution, because we are on the eve of the fourth summit and the situation has not changed, unfortunately. We were hoping that the Prime Minister's claim of a special relationship with President

March 11, 1988
Borrowing Authority
Reagan would achieve our goal of a treaty on acid rain pollution abatement.
At least four million tonnes of sulphur dioxide crosses the Canadian-American border each year. That transboundary pollution is damaging our waters, our forests, our agriculture, fish spawning grounds and the fisheries in general. It is also damaging our building structures and monuments. It is damaging human health. The total yearly damage runs into the millions of dollars.
Having listened to the invocations and incantations, and having watched the smoke and mirror performances over the last three years, on the eve of the fourth summit it becomes imperative in this debate to impress upon the Government the need to muster the courage and present a bill for damages to President Reagan when they meet again in April.
Considering the expectations that were raised by the Prime Minister in 1985, this matter can no longer be allowed to drag. Expectations were raised with the Canadian public in this very Chamber a year ago when President Reagan was here. When he left Ottawa that day the Prime Minister proclaimed the event as a breakthrough and a success in terms of acid rain reduction. Since April of last year, after proclaiming there had been a breakthrough, nothing has happened. There has not been a reduction of one ounce in the tonnage of sulphur dioxide that crosses the border between Canada and the United States. The damage is the same, and it continues. Our resources are facing even more damage as a result of this.
Canada has embarked on a program to cut our pollution. The Americans who are downwind from us will benefit from our program. The transboundary pollution from Canada into the United States will be reduced by half between now and 1994. The least we can expect is reciprocity. Since we are not getting this reciprocity under the present Government and the Reagan regime, our only alternative is to present a bill for damages being caused to the Canadian economy, human health and Canadian resources as a whole.
We also want to consider the over-all picture in this debate. While the Government continues to increase taxes, it has not lowered the public debt as it promised to do in the 1984 campaign. The taxes, particularly the invisible federal sales tax, have been increased methodically year by year.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are in fact facing this morning a situation that is something of a paradox concerning the Bill now before us, because the Hon. Member for La Prairie (Mr. Jourdenais) boasted during Question Period of this Conservative Government's prowess in the area of employment. We now find ourselves with a proposal to give the Government authority to borrow an extra $25 billion in order to operate till the end of the year.
To dare claim, as my colleague for La Prairie did, that the employment situation is almost exclusively due to this Government's prowess, is showing misplaced boastfulness, Mr. Speaker, and more still this is misleading Canadians because all the previous governments, including the short-lived conservative ones, always have been at the mercy of the global economic situation.
When the global economic situation was good, jobs were created. But when we are going through a period of recession, global recession, then we have unemployment. And if at this time the Government can show pride, it is not necessarily because of its prowess but rather because of a global economy that is totally favourable and that results in a strong economy, an economy that can create jobs, an economy that normally should be allowing the Government to manage public finance without having to ask for a $25 billion borrowing authority, as we have now.
Mr. Speaker, this is the second time I have an opportunity to rise on this borrowing authority requested by the Government, and as my colleague for Trinity (Mrs. Nicholson) mentioned earlier, this Bill was tabled before the Government came up with its Estimates. As she said this morning, even after examining them I fail to understand why, at a time when the international economy and our domestic economy are in excellent shape, the Government is obliged to ask for an additional $25 billion to be able to run this country.
Mr. Speaker, there has been a lot of bragging about the fact that 1,200,000 jobs have been created since 1984. Normally, those jobs would generate additional revenue for the Government, through taxes. So I fail to understand why the Government wants to maintain a borrowing authority of $25 billion when its revenues are increasing, unless its expenditures are increasing at a tremendous rate as well, since the deficit is going down far less than the Minister of Finance said it would when he tabled his forecasts in previous years.
Mr. Speaker, when I spoke the first time, I said that this Bill was a perfect example of the poor management the Conservative Government has been inflicting on Canadians during the past four years.
I would also like to express my grave concern about the precarious situation in which our youth finds itself, and about the many problems connected with regional disparity in Canada.
As we all know, if the Bill is passed, the Government will be able to increase the national debt by $25.3 billion in the course of the financial year starting on April 1. Twenty five billion may not sound like much, just another loan added to a national debt that is already far too high. At the end of this financial year our national debt will total nearly $3 billion. This works out to a little over $12,000 per Canadian, per year. That is a tremendous burden, Mr. Speaker. It is a serious problem, when we consider that despite the fact that the economy is in very
March 11, 1988

good shape, the Conservative Government keeps increasing our debt.
I have said it before, Mr. Speaker, and I say it again: As a Canadian citizen, I am very concerned about the fact that this Government has failed to take advantage of the excellent economic situation this country has enjoyed in the past four years. Actually, $25.3 billion is far too much for a Government that has undermined the confidence of Canadians by failing to keep its promises. It is an incredible amount of money for a Minister of Finance who in his last Budget made it clear he was totally unqualified to manage the money of Canadian taxpayers. It is incredible, when we consider that with all the money it has borrowed and collected in the form of taxes, and despite the excellent state of the economy, the Conservative Goverment still has nothing to offer the poorest and neediest among us, and especially our youth.
The times we live in demand strong intervention by the federal Government in a number of areas, such as guaranteed income, education and training, quality of life and housing. This Government tends to neglect these serious issues and remains supremely indifferent to the legitimate concerns of Canadian men and women who have to cope with these problems.
Poverty lies at the heart of most of Canada's social problems, including poor health, crime, unsanitary accommodation, family violence and mental illness. The Government cannot continue to maintain that improving the economy will make it possible to bridge the gap between rich and poor. The poor are not necessarily unemployed. It is because of their jobs pay such low wages that some workers are poor. It is wrong to suggest that society helps everyone when the heads of 55 per cent of poor families in Canada have a paying job.
Families are hit especially hard by poverty. However, the measures contained in the last Budgets and the tax reform have challenged the principle that Governments agree to compensate parents for the costs they incur in raising their children. This Government has partially de-indexed family allowances, lowered the ceiling for elegibility to the child tax credit and eliminated the child exemption.
In another area, the International Year of Shelter for the Homeless has gone by without the Government really dealing with this issue.
In 1986, over 100,000 Canadians were homeless at one time or another. In 1987, the situation did not improve and it may even have worsened. It is estimated that 750,000 more families had an urgent need or decent or affordable housing. In the area of housing, the Conservative Governement has constantly imposed enormous budgetary restrictions, limited elegibility to subsidized housing, thus victimizing low and middle income families, and delegated its responsabilities to the provinces.
Throughout Canada, the streets, the water mains and the bridges are cracking up and becoming corroded and distorted because they are put to a greater use than previously and less
Borrowing Authority
maintenance is being done on them. While the Federation of Canadian Municipalities is requesting new federal initiatives to provide part of the $15 billion investment necessary to modernize municipal services, the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) has stated that municipalities should increase the water rates paid by consumers to repair the water supply system.
As a former mayor, Mr. Speaker, I can say that I intend to move a motion in the near future to ask for a national water purification program and a municipal toxic waste elimination program to provide assistance to the municipalities, which, because of weak federal or provincial legislation, are not necessarily responsible for all the pollution, caused, even though this unfortunately comes under their jurisdiction at the present time.
Also, we had to wait nearly two years following the cancellation of the Manpower Adjustment Program before the Government introduced its Older Worker Adjustment Program. In 1982, 4.8 per cent of the unemployed had been without jobs for over a year. In late 1987, this proportion had increased to nearly 20 per cent, which represents about
200,000	Canadians. On the other hand, 158,000 people had been looking for jobs for a period ranging from 27 to 52 weeks. To the number of those who are chronically unemployed, we must add the 400,000 people who are considered fringe workers. At the end of 1987, there were in Canada 55,000 disillusioned unemployed workers who had stopped looking for jobs, feeling that their chances of finding jobs were pratically non-existent. Faced with this serious problem, the Tory Government continued just the same to reduce the funds allocated for the Formal Training Program, while subsidizing jobs in the private sector.
When the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) brags about the results his Government has achieved with job creation, he overlooks the fact that these jobs are unequally distributed among the provinces, between men and women and among the various age groups. Data collected by Statistics Canada reveal the following discrepancies: Ontario, with 38 per cent of the total labour force in Canada, had bagged 45 per cent of all the jobs created in Canada in 1987. Which means that 62 per cent of the manpower in Canada had to be satisfied with the remaining 55 per cent of the new jobs. While men lay claim to 61 per cent or the majority of all full-time jobs, women hold 71 per cent or most part-time jobs. Part-time workers are paid a lower average hourly salary, about equal to 79 per cent of the salary paid to full-time employees, and often receive no social benefits.
In December 1987, the unemployment rate for our labor force generally was 8.1 per cent, but it was 8.6 per cent among women and only 7.7 per cent among men. For the same month, the unemployment rate among people between 15 and 19 years of age was 13.5 per cent.
In spite of this evidence, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance continues to describe Canada as a country of affluent

men and women driving Le Baron cars and whose portfolios withstood quite well the crash of last Fall. In short, the Minister of Finance feels that everything is fine and dandy in Canada.
He does not seem to realize what it means to be poor in Canada. To be poor in Canada, Mr. Speaker, is to be put at an unfair disadvantage when it comes to housing, education and training, daycare and legal aid services, credit and health care.
Many of the Canadian poor live on welfare. Many others are small-wage earners. The majority of single seniors and single families headed by women have an income that is hundreds and often thousands of dollars below the poverty line. The economic difficulties of this decade have swelled the ranks of the poor and hardened society's reaction to that fact of everyday life. Poverty affects people of all ages, but the saddest thing about existing programs for fighting poverty is that 20 per cent of Canadian children live in an underprivileged environment.
In 1986, Mr. Speaker, 3.7 million Canadians, or 14.9 per cent of the population, lived below the poverty line. Last year, more than 34 per cent of single persons were poor. That amounts to 982,000 Canadians. More than a million children below 16, that is 1,016,000 children, live in poverty. Nearly 57 per cent of the poor in Canada are women, although women account for only 51 per cent of the population. And more than half, or 56 per cent, of single families headed by women are poor.
The number of Canadians with an income below the poverty line rose from 3,475,000 in 1980 to 4,240,000 in 1984. The number has decreased since then, but the 1986 figures were still higher than those of 1980, before the recession, Mr. Speaker.
In 1986, the total income of the poorest 20 per cent of Canadians was only 4.7 per cent of the over all income of the Canadian population. By contrast, the richest 20 per cent had 43 per cent of the over all income, nine times the income of the poorest group.
In spite of these alarming facts, Mr. Speaker, this Government brags so loudly about the people who are benefiting from the improved economic situation that it cannot hear the complaints of those who benefit not at all or very little from it. As a Liberal concerned for the welfare of all Canadians, I reject a plan which is supportive of the well-to-do privileged classes while the poorest and neediest suffer.
The Government still brags about its job creation figures. While the situation is improving, which is quite normal after six years of recovery, there are still over one million unemployed in Canada, but the Government does not seem to care. It regularly cuts back its job creation programs on the assumption that our economy is doing so well that people should be able to find a job without Government assistance. As I have already said, this might be true in certain regions, but it is certainly not the case everywhere in Canada, and it is
certainly not the case for young people, whose unemployment rate is still twice as high as the national average.
Mr. Speaker, if the Bill now before the House was a guarantee that the Government will create jobs for young people, that it will create or implement programs or projects to reduce poverty in Canada, that part of these amounts will be used to improve the quality of life for all Canadians, and more particularly for all young people in Canada, then, Mr. Speaker, I would have no objection to voting for this Bill. However, as we are aware of the wasteful spending which occurs during certain trips and as we know that these $25 billion could be used for purposes which will not benefit all Canadians, we cannot agree to provide this Government with the power to borrow $25 billion more.
