speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I also wish to participate in the debate. The Government is asking us to approve its borrowing measure of more than $25 billion. I believe that that is the largest sum that any Government has ever asked Parliament's permission to borrow. Given the type of deficits accumulated over the years, one can understand that the sum that the Government needs to borrow has progressively increased year after year.
I wish to place on the record, despite some of the statements made by both Conservative and Liberal Party Members, that New Democrats are concerned about the deficit.
Historically, in my own Province of Saskatchewan when a CCF Government was elected in 1944, essentially the province was broke. Yet over the years we were able to bring the economy of the province back up, implement a program of rural electrification, which cost a fair amount of money for Saskatchewan, introduce a system of regional and local hospitals and schools and a road system throughout that huge province.
That was done without leaving large accumulated debts. One of the things that we were proud of in Saskatchewan was that we consistently ran surpluses if not balanced budgets. The same was true during the period 1971 to 1982 when the New Democratic Party formed the Government in Saskatchewan. In those years we ran balanced budgets. It took the election of a Conservative Government in Saskatchewan in 1982 to introduce deficits into Saskatchewan. At the present time, the people of Saskatchewan are burdened with a horrendous debt and an accumulated deficit of several billions of dollars that will take several hundreds of years into the future to pay off.
In looking at the federal debt, one realizes that paying the interest on the debt is one of the largest, if not the largest expenditure of government. There is certainly nothing socialist about paying several million dollars every year on the interest on what the Government owes. As New Democrats we are committed to seeing that the deficit is wiped off the books as quickly as possible and as humanely as possible.
March 11, 1988

It is interesting to note that historically it seems that during periods of Conservative Governments the debt seems to increase. That is certainly true in the United States. Under President Reagan the United States has had the largest deficit in its history. The same can be said of the Government of Margaret Thatcher. Certainly, in the Province of Saskatchewan there has been a debt increase since the Conservatives were elected. One becomes puzzled why this is so. After all, Conservative Governments are noted for cut-backs in government service. The philosophy of the Conservative Government is that government should not play an active role in the society, and Conservative Governments talk in terms of fiscal responsibility and Government living within its means. Indeed, under Conservative Governments generally there is a decrease in government expenditures. Yet the deficit increases. Why?
I think that the answer can be found in the fact that generally under Conservative Governments one finds tax breaks particularly for the wealthy, and that the revenue source for Government decreases under Tory Governments. That is true in the United States, it is true in Great Britain under the Thatcher Government, it certainly was true in Saskatchewan whom the Government of Premier Grant Devine dramatically decreased the taxes that the oil industry had been paying into the coffers of Saskatchewan, and I think it is also true in Canada.
Despite the tax reform introduced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), he still admitted in his papers when he introduced tax reform that there will be some 60,000 well-to-do profitable corporations that will still not pay one cent of tax. Among the 60,000 will be found some smaller companies, but also some of the larger companies. Is it any wonder that there is this large accumulated deficit in Canada when one considers that, in 1983, a teller with the Royal Bank of Canada paid more in taxes than did the Royal Bank of Canada? Although the Royal Bank of Canada, in 1983, had over $360 million in profits, it did not pay one cent in taxes. In fact, it received a tax credit of some $20 million. The Government felt that it was not profitable enough, so it gave the bank a tax credit of some $20 million.
Perhaps one should not single out the Royal Bank of Canada because it certainly was not the only one. Most other banks did not pay a cent in tax. Most trust companies did not pay a cent in tax. Certainly none of the insurance companies with billions of dollars in profits paid a cent in tax. No wonder we have a deficit like the one we have.
Some folk will say that the reason for the large deficit is that we have been living beyond our means or that the social programs in Canada are too rich. Tory spokespersons like to indicate that the Government has been handing out money to the poor, spending too much money on education, health, housing, and other social programs, and that is why we have a deficit. However, when we look at what we in Canada spend as a percentage of our gross domestic product on social programs,
Borrowing Authority
compared with other industrialized nations in the world, we find that we are the second lowest. We spend less on things like housing, education, maternity care, job creation, pensions, unemployment insurance, and so forth than Holland, Germany, Denmark, Sweden, Norway, Great Britain, France, and Italy. Countries that have fewer resources than we have, countries that have much larger populations in much smaller areas, countries that have a much older population, all spend a greater amount on social programs as a percentage of gross domestic product than we do in Canada.
For me to hear people say that we are living beyond our means in Canada is something that I just cannot accept. I cannot accept that when I see in my home City of Regina young children going hungry. Here in the bread-basket of the world we have young kids going hungry. In our largest cities we see the homeless, people who cannot afford to put a decent roof over their heads because they do not have the income. We see line-ups at food banks from coast to coast. Surely to say that we are living beyond our means is really to crack a cruel joke.
The fact of the matter is that we are not living beyond our means. There is real poverty in the country. In a country so blessed with richness and wealth there are over 4 million people who are living below the poverty line, who are living in poverty. For Conservative spokespersons to claim that we are living beyond our means is nothing but propaganda. It is not true; it is not true at all.
Essentially we heard from the Minister of Finance as he presented his Budget and as he justified his borrowing authority Bill, that under the leadership of the Conservative Government the economy of Canada is doing quite well. Of course it is all relative. Indeed there are fewer people who are unemployed today than there were in 1984. That is very true. However, we must not forget that, compared with the United States, for example, our unemployment is still quite high, unacceptably high.
Fet us step back one second. When inflation was out of control in the late 1970s or early 1980s, industrialized countries decided in a joint effort to wrestle inflation to the ground. They did it by increasing the interest rate, in essence by taking the steam out of the economy and forcing the western economy into a recession. Well, it certainly brought down the inflation rate. Right now it is running at some 4 per cent, but this was done at the price of an economic slow-down and at the price of millions of men and women in the western world losing their jobs, being thrown on the heap of unemployed. It was particularly severe for working Canadian men and women.
Our unemployment rate was one of the highest of western industrialized countries. The recovery from the recession in Canada was slower than other industrialized countries. When the Conservatives came to power in 1984 we still had an unduly high unemployment rate. The recovery from the recession had been slower in Canada, in part because of the

March 11, 1988
Borrowing Authority
type of economy we have. A large part of our economy depends upon the export of basic raw materials. When there is an economic recovery, the suppliers of raw materials are the countries that experience the recovery as being slower than in other more industrialized countries. It took a while for the recovery in western economies to be felt in Canada.
In a sense the Conservatives were lucky that they were elected in a period when the recovery started to occur. Yes, unemployment has declined dramatically in Canada. The Minister of Finance is happy to point out that it has declined more rapidly in Canada than in other industrialized countries. However, one begins to wonder whether or not it was as a result of the actions of the Government. It might very well be that the Conservatives were lucky to be elected in a period when the recovery was occurring.
We also wonder how a Government, which does not believe in becoming involved in the economy and which has a basic philosophy of laissez-faire, could take credit for the economic recovery. In fact, the Minister stated that in more or less those terms when he appeared before the finance committee last week. He said: "We cannot really take credit for this; it is the industry out there that has created the jobs".
One could wonder what sort of economic situation we would be in, had we had a Government which believed that the public sector had a role to play and that indeed we could devise economic strategies to create jobs. In fact, one could wonder how much better off Canadians would be, particularly in regions where we still have 10 per cent, 15 per cent, and 20 per cent unemployment, if we had a Government which believed that the public sector had a role to play and had some economic strategy to make certain that economic recovery occurred in all regions of the country.
We have asked the Government, as part of an initiative to help create more jobs, to lower the interest rate by 1 or 2 per cent. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) calls us irresponsible. In fact, in committee the other day, the Minister of Finance told my colleague that what we were saying was garbage. The funny thing is that when the Minister of Finance was in opposition, he was also calling for the Government to lower the interest rate. It must have been garbage back then as well. It is amazing how the Liberals and Tories change their tune when they cross from one side of the floor to the other. When the Tories were in opposition, they were calling for a lower interest rate. Now that they are in government, they say they cannot do it. When the Liberals were in power, they said they could not lower the interest rate, but now that they are in opposition they are, in turn, calling for a lower interest rate. It is amazing how the Liberals and Tories flip back and forth on the question. We suggest that we can lower the interest rate by 1 or 2 per cent without causing undue inflationary pressure.
The Minister of Finance says that inflation at 4 per cent is unacceptable. I agree with him. But it is not the interest rate
that is keeping inflation at 4 per cent, it is the action of the very Government. The Government has increased taxes, increased public transportation costs, fuel, oil and gas taxes. We have seen property tax increase. Tuition fees for postsecondary education, tobacco and alcohol taxes and electricity costs have all increased. The present Government has also introduced a 10 per cent telecommunications tax. These tax increases, many of them imposed by the federal Government, some of them by the provinces and local municipalities because of the cut-backs in transfer payments, have resulted in prices going up and an inflation rate of 4 per cent. It is not because of low interest rates, nor is it because workers are demanding higher wages. In fact, the wage level has been below the inflationary level. Those are not the targets anymore. The reasons for high inflation are the revenue and tax grabs by the federal Government.
Yes, we can have a lower interest rate. Yes, the cost of production can be lower in Canada so that we can be competitive with our trading partners, who pay lower interest costs as a cost of their production. Unfortunately, we have a government that had its head in the sand and is not providing the economic type of leadership that Canada surely deserves. Canada deserves economic leadership. The poor in this country deserve some leadership, and they have not received it from this Government.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1988-89 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have this opportunity to speak on the Government's Bill C-109, the Bill in which the Government asks for the authority to borrow $25.3 billion, almost the amount of the deficit. That is what the Government is borrowing. It is necessary for us to give some attention to what the Government may do with the money and how it will use what it gets from the taxpayers.
There is the old principle that you should look at what a person does rather than what he says. The same applies to government. How the Government spends the taxpayers' money demonstrates where its priorities really are. That is what we have to examine in this debate about borrowing $25.3 billion.
The Budget that proceeded this borrowing Bill was fairly skimpy on information. There was a great deal of self congratulation in it, pages and pages of glowing expensively printed remarks about what a fine Government it is. There was much less information than usual about the details of the Government's plans and priorities. However, there is some information on which I want to focus, particularly in two areas. They present a very striking contrast and they show where the priorities of the Government really are. The first area is defence in the general sense and, in particular, the nuclear powered attack submarines.
This year the Government plans to spend $23 million simply on preparation, making the plans and so on, to buy these attack submarines. The total cost of the submarines will be somewhere between $7 billion and $15 billion. Some estimates are higher. The Government used to have a lower estimate, but
March 11, 1988

it got laughed out of that. The $7 billion to $15 billion range depends on whether we look at the bare bones submarines themselves or whether we include the support facilities and the necessary base.
The other area I want to look at is child care. Some of the money from this borrowing Bill will be spent on the Government's child care plans. The plans are to spend about $5.4 billion over seven years on child care. At first, $5.4 billion sounds generous. It sounds almost like the cost of three or four submarines. We have to look closer. The Government's plan appears to be comprehensive on the surface, and there is a significant amount of money involved. The Government will spend $2.3 billion over this seven years on tax breaks for parents with children. The Government will spend $3 billion for capital and operating costs for child care centres and $100 million for special initiatives for research and pilot projects among special groups.
One thing which is a matter of common experience is that tax programs are generally the least effective way of creating public programs because it gives the Government very little power to direct where the money that comes from tax breaks will be spent. In other words, spending what are called tax expenditures. In this case, the tax expenditures are particularly hypocritical. The Government, at the same time as it undertakes to spend this money on day care through tax breaks, will be cutting family benefits. By 1991 these family benefit cuts will have taken $1.5 billion out of the pockets of families.
Let us take a closer look at both tax breaks. Together they will amount to a total of $2.4 billion. If this money were used to create new child care spaces, an additional 170,000 Canadian children would have spaces. That is not the way it is going to be done. The tax programs mean that there will be a refundable child tax credit with a maximum of $200 a year per child. That is not enough to pay for even informal non-market, non-receipted child care. It is a drop in the bucket compared to the cost of child care these days. It is not enough to enable a couple to make the decision to forego the income from one of them working so that that he or she can stay home to take care of a child or children. It offers a little extra fuel to the so-called underground market, whatever kind of unreceipted day care may be offered on a very informal basis, with no assurance of quality for the parents and no assurance of quality for the kids, but the parents are forced to take it because that is all there is. It is called choice, but it is a situation of no choice.
Second, the doubling of the child care expense deduction for receipted child care sounds generous, but in reality, on the basis of past experience only a minority, the well-to-do minority of families, can benefit from this amount. In 1984 only 15 per cent of families could afford to save money this way. It does not work for the big majority of the population. The average family could only take advantage of one-half of the deduction that is being provided, one that will give, of course, full benefit to the wealthier families. This is another way of rewarding those who already have much more income than most people in this country.
Borrowing Authority
The next important area in this program is the capital and operating grants. The system the Government has proposed has led some day care people to call it a child care limitation plan. In the past, under Canada Assistance, there was no ceiling set, no cap set on how much could be done by the shared programs in which the Government participated to 50 per cent. But now there is a cap set and the government objective is to create 200,000 spaces during the next seven years. That is a slower rate, a far slower rate than the rate at which they were created during the years since 1974. In other words, there will be a slowdown in the creation of new spaces for child care; that is, for licensed, receiptable, quality child care. Furthermore, by the end of the seven years, the operating funds provided by the Government will have been reduced to less than $2 per child per day.
What will we have at the end of seven years for this program? We will not have this Government, of course, but if this program continues, what will we have at the end of seven years? There will be two million children-this is the Government's figure-still without access to licensed day care spaces. There will be no action on the kind of maternal or parental leave provisions that might make home care a reality. There will be an expensive tax deduction and credit program that helps rich families more than ordinary families, and a program that fails to provide real choices or real assistance to the majority of families. In short, it is a typical Tory program that helps the well-to-do with the tax money that comes at the expense of ordinary Canadians, a program that fails to deliver its promises.
I would like to direct attention to the Minister of National Defence's nuclear-attack subs. This is a Budget which involves spending $23 million this year for the preliminary planning work, the project-definition phase, but the rumours are that that has to be pushed this year because DND is desperately trying to get the contracts firmly in place before the Tory Government is defeated in the next election. The original price tag for the total project was said to be $5 billion. That caused great laughter throughout Canada and throughout the western world since, obviously, that was more like half price for 10 to 12 subs.
The Government has discovered that the subs in fact need shore bases. It appears that it left that out. Shore bases cost money. So the total project cost now, according to independent critics which the Government does not answer in any detail, is somewhere between $10 billion and $15 billion. Those are the costs.
We know that the Government's child care program is not going to work. The question is, will the subs work. The question is what will they do. Well, they will travel under the ice. That is quite true. They will travel under the ice. The question then is, what for. What work will they do when they have travelled under the ice?

March 11, 1988
Borrowing Authority
The Minister's original rationale was, he said, to protect our sovereignty in northern waters and to protect us against the supposed Soviet cruise missile attack. Well, as Professor James Eayers who has studied this matter for many years said, and I quote:
It is the most bizarre decision in Canadian weapons policy since the premier
of British Columbia bought two submarines originally built in Seattle for
Chile.
That fantastic decision was made during World War I. It was supposed to protect British Columbia coastal fishing from raids by German ships, Germany being on the other side of the Atlantic.
Well, this is the World War III equivalent, I guess, by our Minister of National Defence (Mr. Beatty), of the folly of World War I. The decision that was made in World War I was to protect the citizens of British Columbia from a non-existent threat. But there at least was then a real war, and it was hot. Today's decision takes place in the midst of a war that is real, but cold. It is real because people like the Minister of National Defence work very hard at keeping it going.
Canada has the doubtful distinction of having a Defence Minister who is more of a hawk than Ronald Reagan, and is insisting on Canadian subs which neither NATO nor the United States have asked for. Granted, if we offered to donate them to Lord Carrington, he would say thank you, but this was never considered a necessary part of defence.
The estimate of the Soviet forces and the Soviet threat in the White Paper are even more exaggerated than the estimates in the Pentagon's propaganda. President Reagan on the one hand is willing to discuss with the Russians the possibility of limited cuts to nuclear weapons in the intermediate-range and long-range departments, but the Defence Minister will have nothing to do with discussion of arms reductions with the Russians. He is not even willing to begin seriously discussing nuclear weapons free reduction or exclusion or limitation in the zone of the Arctic.
He should recall by his reading what was said by a well-known leader of defence, Sir Winston Churchill, some years ago. It is always better to jaw-jaw than to war-war. Even Churchill, though he was a good leader in war, preferred to negotiate where there was an opportunity to do that. We have a Defence Minister who would rather spend, spend than negotiate. In fact, he would rather spend, spend than have an arms reduction.
His spending will increase the chance of war. These attack subs, whether they are nuclear or otherwise, do not have a genuine defensive role for Canada. The Arctic waters of Canada are not and will not be the forward staging areas for some supposed Soviet attack. They are not suitable. They are narrow, they are shallow, they are ice clogged and most submarine-launched cruise missiles such as might be feared from those subs do not have the range to hit American targets from the Canadian Arctic. The Russian ballistic-missile submarines do not have to come near Canadian waters to
launch their missiles. They can do it more conveniently from the Atlantic or the Pacific.
Using these subs for coastal defence does not make much sense. How does a sub warn off surface ships as effectively as a frigate can? It just does not make sense. But what may be the Government's logic is something far more dangerous than that to peace.
On February 3, Vice Admiral John Anderson of the Canadian navy testified before the House of Commons defence committee. He told the committee that in times of heightened tension, Canadian nuclear attack submarines might be sent to attack Soviet strategic submarines. That is about as dangerous a strategy as can be imagined. It is part of the United States navy doctrine, the so-called forward maritime strategy. What it means is that the United States, or in this case the United States and Canada, or by a trade off, the United States and Canada together, would send large numbers of nuclear submarines and aircraft carriers into the Soviet northern waters at the first hint of any crisis. Their mission would be to sink Soviet strategic submarines in the Barents Sea as soon as there was any outbreak or skirmish of conventional war. In other words, as soon as there may be a war anywhere with conventional weapons, we might have Canada with the United States initiating a nuclear war, which most Governments and experts, both in our country and elsewhere, have admitted would not allow survivors. In other words, a nuclear war is not a war in the conventional sense that there is a winner and a loser. It is an exchange of weapons with the result that all would be losers. This would be the result of the American forward maritime strategy, which is the only logical use for the proposed Canadian nuclear submarines.
That strategy is a most dangerous military proposal, probably the most dangerous the Reagan Government has prepared, and we should not be going along with it. It makes war more likely, not less likely.
We have to look at what the Government does with our money, not what it says, when we consider lending it the money. It announced a day care program that would leave hundreds of thousands of Canadian children without day care. If, as the NDP suggests, all the money in this program had been used to create new spaces, we estimate that at least
170,000	more spaces would have been created over the life of the program. Instead, the Government spends the money we need for child care on nuclear attack submarines. Those submarines make nuclear war and the end of the human race much more likely. This is a very poor Budget and a very poor reason for borrowing $25.3 billion.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for his question. The Canadian Government has proposed that these submarines could replace American submarines to make the American submarines available for attack on the Russian submarines. It is also clear that a plan for armament of the Canadian submarines may be developed or revised once the proposal is under way.
The nuclear component of the subs is nuclear power, not nuclear missiles or any of those things used in American, British and Soviet submarines. However, those submarines are described as attack submarines, therefore their target is clearly Soviet submarines.
The point at which I say it increases the risk of war is that if there is some little skirmish and the Soviet Government knows that Canadian submarines, either by replacing American submarines or by attacking themselves, may destroy the Soviet submarines, it may very well act on the principle of: Use them or lose them. It might be prompted to initiate nuclear war in order not to be wiped out by a first strike of NATO forces. That is why that kind of provocative armament makes nuclear war more likely and peace less likely.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1988-89 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to make a few remarks on the Government request to borrow some $25 billion. I want to suggest that the Government's priorities, as revealed in the Budget tabled last month, are wrong. The Budget essentially says to Canadians who are unemployed or having a very difficult time making ends meet that, "I'm all right, Jack". That just is not good enough.
It boasts about bringing unemployment down. We heard more boasts about that this morning. Certainly we on this side of the House are pleased to see any reduction in unemployment. However, on Vancouver Island we have exactly the same number of unemployed today as we had in September of 1984. Nothing has changed. Some 35,000 people are still listed in official statistics as being unemployed and the Budget does absolutely nothing about that.
I want to mention a couple of specifics, first regarding small craft harbours. That issue is of particular concern in my riding but it is also of concern in ridings on both coasts and, indeed, in the other parts of Canada. Last spring the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Oceans held a number of hearings on this issue. In June it submitted its report, and I would like to refer to that.
The report says that investigations by the committee reveal that the level of effort dedicated to the repair and maintenance
Borrowing Authority
of federal small craft harbours is inadequate, which is inconsistent with the stated Government goal of providing increased safety for our fishermen and protecting their material investments. In the short term, this inadequacy will prolong disruptions to commercial fishing, endanger harbour users or their property, and result in increased repair or maintenance costs when necessary work is delayed. In the long term the level of effort will neither protect the value of the assets nor sustain the harbours in safe and usable condition for those they serve.
The report went on to say that the committee heard testimony from Department of Fisheries and Oceans' officials that the minimum requirement to have all commercial fishing in recreational harbours under the administration of the Department and meet the small craft harbour guidelines is $120 million a year for the next five years. It was also indicated to the committee that should the small craft harbours program be required to continue at the present base funding of $48.5 million, there would be the inevitable closure of at least 150 harbours within five years.
Those very serious facts have been addressed in a most inadequate fashion by the Minister, his Department, and the Government. Instead of bringing forward a realistic Budget with projections over a number of years to deal with this problem, we have instead a phoney small craft harbour revitalization program which is really a dressed-up system of privatization that will provide an initial grant to municipalities or user groups, after which they will have the responsibility for maintenance and operation. It is a way for the federal Government to get out from under its historic responsibility of maintaining the infrastructure across Canada.
At least one community in my constituency has looked at this whole situation, and they feel it is just not feasible for them to get involved in taking over responsibility for a harbour. They have looked at the statistics and seen that when other communities have done this, they have inevitably lost money. That is not surprising. I do not think that our harbours should necessarily be money-makers. We do not expect that our roads be money-makers, and our airports are not moneymakers. Why are we loading that burden upon small communities which depend upon these harbours for their fishing industry and, in many cases, their tourism and recreational industry? Why do we try to shuffle federal responsibility on to communities or user groups?
I want to mention some specific harbours in my riding. The harbour of Sooke on the west coast of Vancouver Island is protected by a well known land form called the Whiffen Spit, a very beautiful piece of land which stretches out and protects the harbour. In recent years it has been subjected to a great deal of erosion. There has been a jurisdictional dispute between the federal Government, which has responsibility for maintaining the harbour, and the provincial government, which actually owns the land.

March 11, 1988
Borrowing Authority
Because these two levels of government have not been able to get together to solve a real problem for this community, the Whiffen Spit is eroding very badly. I visited it not long ago. There is a gap in the spit some 10 feet deep and 500 feet long. That means that storms will be able to move right through the spit which traditionally provided a very effective breakwater.
That will do damage to government facilities at the small craft harbour floats, to private marinas, and to the Uplands property owners. It will make it very difficult for the local mill to get barges in and out and to maintain the mill. It is essential that the two levels of government get together and find some way of solving the problem of the Whiffen Spit in the interests of the total community. So far we have not seen any real action on that.
There is also the situation of Cowichan Bay. A year ago I wrote to the Minister and pointed out that there is a very difficult situation there, that the breakwater is inadequate and that repairs should be undertaken immediately to extend it and provide additional protection to what the present breakwater gives. Admittedly, it will be an expensive proposition, but we are talking about the need to protect hundreds of thousands of dollars of both public and private investment. We received no positive response from the Minister on this. This past winter a very bad storm did a great deal of damage in Cowichan Bay, and the community is now looking to the Government in hopes of getting some federal assistance to rebuild.
In Ladysmith they need federal help to upgrade their Department of Fisheries and Oceans small craft harbour, but have been told that they can only get help if they form a local harbour authority and go for the government privatization program which it calls revitalization.
It is the Government's refusal to accept its historic responsibilities and its attempts to get out from under that makes us very leery of giving the Government permission to borrow $25 billion.
In Port Renfrew, another community on the west coast of Vancouver Island, there is a Transport Canada wharf which is urgently in need of repairs to bring it up to standard. These repairs will be expensive, costing some $900,000. Instead of looking at possibilities for increasing the use of this wharf if it is brought up to standard, Transport Canada simply decided to write it off, saying that the present level of usage does not justify that expense.
I have received correspondence from the community of Snug Cove on Bowen Island in another riding. There is a proposal there to get rid of the Department of Transport's floats and replace them with a private development. Local people are very concerned about what kind of access they will have and what the effect on the environment will be.
Speaking of the environment, we must question the commitment of the Government to taking action on the environment. We have been drifting along and acting as though everything is going okay with the environment while the environmental
crisis is mounting in Canada and around the world. In the last few months we have seen a great deal of evidence that pulp mills are discharging toxic wastes which have a very severe effect upon the environment and marine life.
In my riding there is a pulp mill at Crofton. Some of the tests done there showed that oysters and crabs there had above safe levels of 2378TCDD, one of the most dangerous toxins known to humanity. We have not taken the action with regard to that toxin or others which is required. There is a whole range of toxins which are not even being adequately tested. The Government does not have the facilities to do the tests in the short length of time which this urgency requires. It has not put the muscle into enforcing environmental standards which the health, safety, and environment of Canadians demands. That raises questions about granting the Government this borrowing authority.
With regard to Canada's commitment to development assistance, we remember that when the Government was first elected the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) made a solemn declaration at the United Nations on behalf of Canadians that we were going to reach .7 per cent of our GNP by 1990. Since then, of course, there has been one retreat after another from that figure. We are now talking about possibly reaching .7 per cent by the 21st century. Last year when the Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade studied Canada's development assistance policy and the Government's commitment in that area it said:
We doubt that the current plan to hold the ratio steady at 0.5 per cent until 1990 and then increase it sharply to 0.6 per cent in the following five years is realistic, particularly considering that we are now at a level slightly below 0.5 per cent.
We are concerned that Canada may find itself once more in the position of abandoning its commitments. In the Committee's view, a plan is needed that would take us to the 0.6 per cent level in 1995-96 by steady, achievable annual increments. Accordingly, the Committee recommends that progress towards achieving the 0.6 per cent target in 1995-96 should begin in the 1988-89 fiscal year, rather than the current plan of fiscal year 1990-91, and proceed by steady annual increases. We estimate that would bring the ODA/GNP ratio to 0.53 per cent in fiscal year 1990-91.
In the just-released government strategy paper Sharing our Future, the Government rejected this recommendation which was made by the Conservative members of the committee. The Liberal member and myself had recommended that the Government should move toward its original commitment of 0.7 by 1990. That was too much for the Conservative members. They were concerned that unless some action was taken our percentage of development assistance would not increase so that by the 1990s there would be a steep increase and Canada would once again welsh on its commitments. We are concerned about this refusal to take our commitments to development assistance seriously. There are crying needs for development in other parts of the world, including Africa, Asia, Central and South America. Canada can be a real world leader because, while we are doing considerable already, we could do many other things to help countries reduce their debts and reach self sufficiency in food production. Much more
March 11, 1988

needs to be done, and that is what we as a nation should be doing.
The Government's attitude that it need not push toward the 0.7 per cent goal, or even work in increments toward reaching the 0.6 per cent goal, is unconscionable in the face of world needs. At the same time, Canada has a government that is dedicated to borrowing billions of dollars to purchase nuclear submarines.
We also witnessed the kind of Government profligacy as detailed in this morning's story about a one-night stop in an Ontario city where the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) will be spending $1,900 without even having a public meeting. Profligate spending on expensive and dangerous toys like nuclear submarines does not contribute to world peace or Canadian security and at the same time neglects vital interests at home. The Government is not dealing with the problems of unemployment in the regions, nor maintaining the infrastructure of industries, such as our fishing industry with small craft harbours. It is not fulfilling the commitments it should in this hurting and hungry world. That is why we have great difficulty with this request to borrow money.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1988-89 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 rise to debate the Government's request to borrow $25 billion to cover some of the shortfall in the Budget that was presented just over a month ago. I do so in the context of my riding in Saskatchewan because people in that area are curious about the Government's expenditures and its handling of the economy.
Last year, inflation was some 4.5 per cent. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) has suddenly decided that it is extremely important to fight inflation and is doing so by keeping interest rates high. In turn, high interest rates have led to an increase in the Canadian dollar by 12 per cent or 13 per cent in the last year. People living in rural areas who produce for an export-price related market will have decreased incomes.
For example, people in my riding who produce grains and oilseeds and whose sales are made in American dollars will face a decrease in sales of some 11 per cent to 12 per cent as a result of the Government's policy with regard to interest rates. People who export beef and pork to the United States will receive 12 per cent or 13 per cent less for those exports because they are dealing in U.S. funds.
There are a number of manufacturers of farm machinery in my riding who primarily export to the United States. It is more difficult for them to export into the United States as the Canadian dollar strengthens and the value of those exports drop accordingly. As a result, some of those companies have been forced to lay off even more workers.
The general tenure of the economy in my part of the country is one of decline. The fight against inflation in rural Saskatchewan has meant a great deal of deflation. Farm land prices
Borrowing Authority
have declined by as much as 50 per cent in my area in the past five years, primarily since the Government came to power. Inflation is not the problem. There are towns and villages in my constituency which have 20 or 30 good quality houses for sale because there is no one to live in them. The prices for such houses have declined by as much as 50 per cent in the last six years which I suggest represents deflation, not inflation.
The Government is mistaken if it believes it can fight inflation with a high interest rate policy. It is a lose-lose situation for my constituents. Since they have lost on the income side by some 12 per cent or 13 per cent, they must borrow money to keep in business but find that interest rates have increased by one per cent to 1.25 per cent in the last year. Therefore, they must pay more money to stay in business. Their income has decreased because of the Government's economic policies and their cost of staying in business is increasing because interest rates are rising according to Government policy.
The Government often talks about win-win situations. Its approach to the economy and the management of the Budget for people in my part of the country is definitely a lose-lose situation. Of course, we cannot all be consistent winners in an economic program. In order for someone to gain an advantage, another must make a sacrifice. In our case, the Minister of Finance has developed a growing economy in an area with which he is more familiar. Unemployment is going down in the Toronto area, and I understand that inflation is rising as property values increase and a hot investment climate continues. However, that is not the case in the West, the Prairies, the North, eastern or Atlantic Canada. The Government should be fighting a war against deflation rather than inflation.
The $25 billion which the Government seeks in borrowing authority will essentially go to pay off the cost of previously borrowed money. Many businesses and farms in my part of the country have been in this kind of financing position for a few years. Ultimately most of them have had to quit.
The net public debt at the end of last fiscal year was $264 billion. We are into the last few weeks of the 1987-88 fiscal year, which means we can add approximately $30 billion as the deficit for this past year. That brings the accumulated deficit the Government is leaving us with in the neighbourhood of $300 billion. Even if the Government is able to borrow money at 8 per cent or 9 per cent to keep paying for that accumulated deficit, that debt, which makes up just about 52 per cent of our Gross National Product on an annual basis, the amount of money the Government wants permission to borrow is not quite enough to pay the interest on that accumulated debt. The $25 billion will barely do that.
I only point that out because I have a lot of constituents, some of whom have been in this situation. A lot of them have watched relatives, friends and neighbours become involved in a similar kind of situation over the last number of years where at

March 11, 1988
Illicit Drugs Promotion
the end of the year they could not pay any of the debt and had to go to the bank, credit union or relatives to borrow money to keep the accumulated debt going for another year. That is basically what we are trying to do. This request by the Government to be given another $25 billion of borrowing power is to permit it to stay afloat for the coming year. The amount in taxes it is receiving will not meet the expenditures which the Government itself has set.
That seems a little strange coming from a Minister of Finance who tells us the problem he faces is a problem of inflation. The textbook definition of inflation is "too many dollars chasing too few goods". Does it not seem ironic that we are borrowing another $25 billion to add to the amount of dollars we are using to chase inadequate government services? Does it not seem ironic that a Government which is worried about inflation would do this sort of thing? Some members of the Government recently attacked me when I made a speech on this matter earlier in the second reading debate. The Hon. Member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes) said his Government was doing a good job, that this was nothing like the radical spending that took place under what he called the "NDP-Liberal alliance" back in the 1970s.
History books do not record any such NDP-Liberal alliance. The Hon. Member referred to the early 1970s. I would like to direct the attention of the House to the record presented by the Minister of Finance when he presented his fiscal plan on February 10, page 96. We see that in 1971-72, at the beginning of that period of this alleged plot, with the NDP forcing the Liberals into all sorts of rapid expenditures and expansion, the net public debt as a percentage of the GNP was 20.5 per cent. That was fairly high. As we went through that two or three years, it dropped. The first year it went down to 19.9 per cent. The following year it dropped to 18.5 per cent. At the end of the period it was at 16.8 per cent. That was from a starting point of 20.5 per cent. If the New Democratic Party had very much influence on the Liberal administration at that time, I submit it was a very good influence because it substantially brought down the proportion of public debt to the Gross National Product.
The Liberals were forced by this Party to follow a certain amount of proper expenditure programs, and were putting government funds into items and projects that would create growth. I think it should be noted that at the beginning of that period the Gross National Product was some $97 billion. At the end of that period, it was at $152 billion, a growth in excess of 50 per cent. That was because of following some of the advice of the New Democrats in that period of time.
I will complete my remarks by simply saying that I find it very strange that the Government persists in trying to fight inflation when, for most of the regions of this country, including my own, the problem is deflation, debt, lower prices, lower incomes and higher costs because the interest rates in this country are far too high.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   CRIMINAL CODE MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as we all know, although the use of narcotics and some other drugs is now illegal, literature promoting the use of drugs, instruments and kits which facilitate their use, can be bought freely in stores or head shops specialized in the sale of such paraphernalia.

The national drug strategy that was announced last May is proof of our commitment to specific undertakings that were made in the Speech from the Throne as solemn promises to the families and parents of Canada. For example, we are dedicated in our intent to eradicate the vast profits that are to be made from the trafficking in illicit drugs by the presentation of the proceeds of crime legislation in Bill C-61.
At the time of its introduction, this legislation received unanimous support from all sides of this House and I, for one, welcome its consideration in committee and speedy return to this Chamber for early passage. Hitting the offender in his or her pocket-book is the only realistic way of terminating the cycle of enterprise crime. More profits breed more crime. We are profoundly concerned about this problem.
There is a dichotomy evident, on the one hand, in the clear statement enunciated in the national drug strategy and, on the
March 11, 1988

other hand, the continued existence of businesses that apparently flourish on the merchandising of so-called drug paraphernalia. A consistent message is fundamental to a successful initiative against drug abuse. There is no room for the impressionable in society, especially our youth, to feel that drug use is acceptable social behaviour. That is the message these entrepreneurs attempt to convey.
The thrust of Bill C-264 is to criminalize any dealings such as importing or selling drug paraphernalia which is defined by the legislation as an "instrument for illicit drug use". This in turn is defined as:
-anything designed primarily or intended under the circumstances for
consuming or to facilitate the consumption of an illicit drug.
The question I would ask is, to whom does the intention apply, that is, does it apply to the seller or to the buyer? Despite the obvious good intentions of the sponsor of this Bill, the Hon. Member for Mississauga North (Mr. Horner), I am concerned that this definition may create a field day for inventive members of the Criminal Defence Bar. That is not to say that members of the Defence Bar are criminals. I wish to be very clear that when one attaches two adjectives to a noun, as did my friend, the Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap), earlier in the day, it is not to be seen that members of the Bar are criminals but rather members of the Criminal Law Defence Bar. This would then result in the initiative being ineffective. We must consider any legislation very carefully, especially in this era which is more and more being shaped by the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. I am not suggesting that we are paralysed from acting decisively.
I am simply saying that our effort must be consistent with the constitutional rights enshrined in the Charter. Since we can always learn from the experience of others, I suggest we might look at the British experience.
The Parliament of the United Kingdom recently passed "drug paraphernalia" legislation. It is contained in the Drug Trafficking Offences Act 1986 which came into force on January 12, 1987. The major part of that legislation is similar to our proceeds of crime legislation, Bill C-61, which provides for the seizure, freezing and forfeiture of the proceeds of drug trafficking, including assets that are physically situated in Canada. It is interesting to note that Canadian assets can be taken into account for the purposes of a confiscation order made by a British court. Section 34 of the British statute which deals with drug paraphernalia states:
(1) Any person who supplies or offers to supply any article which may be used or adapted to be used (whether by itself or in combination with another article or other articles) in the administration by any person of a controlled drug to himself or another, believing that the article (or the article as adapted) is to be so used in circumstances where the administration is unlawful, is guilty of an offence.
Hypodermic syringes or any part thereof are specifically exempted from the operation of this provision by subsection (2). Assuming the evidence establishes a belief that the
Illicit Drugs Promotion
administration of the substance, for instance, heroin, is illegal, one wonders why this exemption for hypodermic syringes was created. It may have some connection with the growing AIDS epidemic that is aggravated by individuals sharing needles for "shooting-up" purposes. The supply of articles for the purpose of preparing a controlled substance for administration is the subject matter of the prohibition in subsection (3). As in Canada, the lawful administration of controlled substances is defined by regulation.
The breadth of those prohibitions is potentially very wide in that they catch every imaginable article in existence that can be employed or adapted for use in the administration or preparation of illicit drugs. The limitation in the provision is created by the requirement that the person who supplies believes that the article is to be employed in either the administration or preparation of administration of a controlled drug. This would appear to be a subjective test which I admit may be quite difficult to prove.
Because of the recent passage of this legislation, experience in the British case has not been able to tell us how useful this approach will be. It may be that an objective test would have been a more effective basis for belief, that is, where there are reasonable grounds to believe that the article will be used for the improper purpose. That would mean that even in situations where the purchaser does not intend to employ the article for illicit administration of drugs, the supplier could still be found guilty because all the surrounding circumstances pointed to the creation in the mind of a reasonable man of a likelihood that unlawful use of the article would be taking place. This type of approach would also assist in the use of undercover police operations to detect and prosecute offenders of this enactment.
This legislation from the United Kingdom is a model that bears consideration and examination. It also points to the level of concern in other countries about the problem of drug paraphernalia. I am sure that the working group that has been set up by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) will be able to provide a much fuller analysis of this provision when its report is delivered. I would prefer to await the delivery of this report which will examine all aspects of the problem.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure to have an opportunity to say a few words regarding Bill C-264. This Bill focuses attention on one of the major crises facing our country today, that is, the widespread drug and alcohol abuse that afflicts so many Canadians, and the fact that it is a growing problem. I do not suppose that there are many of us in the House of Commons who do not know someone or know a family where drug abuse has caused a great deal of heartache, severe problems, and has hampered the future of individuals.
In light of those comments, Mr. Speaker, I want to share with you my surprise on a number of occasions when walking into a certain shop on a certain street and noticing in the display cases all types of interesting paraphernalia, little ceramic pipes, holders, syringes, water-pipes, and certain types

March 11, 1988
Illicit Drugs Promotion
of fancy cigarette papers. One can find all types of interesting tidbits. The only thing that those articles can be used for is to roll joints, smoke hash, munch up magic mushrooms, or whatever it is that people might be into. This is all right out in the open. At the side of the room there are many brochures and booklets on how to grow your own marijuana or how to harvest marijuana plants to get the maximum amount of good oil out of them, and on and on. Then one thinks, Mr. Speaker, my goodness, all of this is illegal in Canada. We are not supposed to smoke hashish, eat magic mushrooms, or take LSD.
I went to the library and got a number of recent studies. Those studies list pages and pages of illicit drugs that can probably be bought on any college campus, in any high school, or on many street corners in the City of Ottawa as well as other cities across the country. The descriptions are vivid, and those studies list the fines attached to summary conviction for possession or trafficking. There is page after page and report after report of the illicit drug situation in Canada. The report on drug abuse and availability of illicit drugs in Canada has perhaps 300 pages of descriptions of what happens town by town in terms of the various types of drugs that have been uncovered by police. It is a horrendous problem that we face.
Bill C-264 comes to grips with this incredible hypocrisy. In the head shops around the country there are people who are presumably making a living selling the paraphernalia and gadgetry that goes with smoking illicit substances, eating them, chewing them, rubbing them, or whatever people might do with them, and that this is apparently okay. This Bill says: "Listen, if you are going to manufacture, promote or sell instruments or offer literature for illicit drug use then it will be considered an offence, you will be guilty, and you will be liable on a summary conviction."
I have just been passed a piece of information that reminds me that in the part of the country I come from on the west coast, magic mushrooms are dried in dryers in the laundromats to make things easier. I do not suppose that laundromats are covered in Bill C-264. Perhaps that might be the next stage.
This is not a laughing matter. It is an attempt by an individual to deal with the problem. It does not deal with the problem. We must not get caught up in concerning ourselves with water-pipes or other apparatus. We must ask ourselves what is behind all of this. What has led to increasing numbers of young people in the country taking mind altering substances? What has driven people, particularly young people, to this kind of behaviour?
There are high levels of unemployment in various parts of Canada, about which we were unfortunately reminded today. In many communities, particularly some of the smaller and remote ones, 20 per cent, 30 per cent, and 40 per cent of the population are unemployed. There are incredible divergences
in terms of social guidelines for young people wherein appropriate behaviour or appropriate action is confusing. Job opportunities for young people are limited. Career opportunities for young people are limited. One could go on and on in terms of the very difficult challenges and problems confronting Canadians today, particularly our young people, but I will not do so. One way to deal with the situation has been to lose oneself by using a mind altering drug or by excessive use of alcohol.
When it comes to smoking, the federal Government has decided to take certain steps. These days we are debating a piece of legislation which will hopefully encourage people to smoke less and consequently save tens of thousands of Canadians each year from all the problems associated with smoking. It is a positive initiative which I think most Canadians would applaud.
Dealing with Bill C-264, which I suspect is honourably motivated, and concerning ourselves with pins, water-pipes, and so on surely misses the point. The point is: Why are these shops necessary? Why is there a need for this paraphernalia? What is behind it? I think that is where we should be focusing our energies and efforts as responsible parliamentarians.
This is not to say that the Government does absolutely nothing in this area, but I think the public is demanding that we do more. Federal, provincial, and local Governments, as well as many agencies, should be taking much more affirmative action in terms of setting the stage so that Canadians, particularly younger ones, learn that the need to escape from reality or the real world through mind altering substances is no longer necessary and that they can live and develop their lives as productive and contributory citizens. At that point we will know that we have been successful in advancing Canada to a more progressive and more civilized country.

-any printed matter describing or depicting, and designed primarily or
intended under the circumstances to promote or glamorize, the production,
preparation or consumption of illicit drugs.
To a great extent the media-and here I do not limit my remarks to the print media but would include the film and television media-have exercised a responsible approach to the publication of material regarding the illicit drug industry. However, there is a segment of the publishing industry which has done much to facilitate the efforts of the drug trafficker through the creation of a mystique surrounding both those who traffic and those who consume illicit drugs. These publishers collectively bear some considerable measure of responsibility for the popularization of so-called soft drugs, and it is toward those publishers that proposed Section 420.1 of Bill C-264 is directed.
The impressionable, the naive, those lacking in self-esteem and self-confidence, are drawn in many ways to experiment with drugs and to be part of a lifestyle they are made to perceive as attractive. Some publishers do not exercise any self-censorship but rather, in seeking to expand their circulation or reputation, do not hesitate to publish that which they would describe as literature-the glorification of successful drug traffickers. I am certain we all support freedom of expression and free exchange of information. However, in a free and democratic society we recognize that reasonable limits may be placed upon such principles.
In a similar fashion small store owners and operators of so-called head shops, specializing in the distribution of devices which have no other legitimate purpose than to facilitate the consumption of drugs, make profit from those who consume illicit drugs. They, too, exploit the victims of organized crime. Make no mistake about it, Mr. Speaker, drug trafficking accounts for the largest share of the criminal transactions of organized crime.
Ultimately all society is the victim of such organized criminal activity. The taxpayer pays for the law enforcement efforts directed at combating and eradicating the illicit drug trade and the cost of imprisoning convicted offenders who trafficked in these substances or committed other crimes in order to obtain money to buy drugs. Of course the victims include those whose lives are forever harmed and destroyed by the consumption of drugs, as well as those who had criminal acts committed against them either by persons under the influence of these substances or by persons who, in order to obtain money to buy drugs, violated their property rights.
On a larger scale, I submit that millions of people unknown to us in the poorer countries of the Third World where many of these drugs are produced are also the victims of this illicit commercial activity. They live in terror, the subjects of drug overlords who hold sway over large territories in South America and Asia. So long as a market for their goods exists in developed nations such as Canada, these drug lords will
Illicit Drugs Promotion
continue to produce. Their markets will not shrink if nothing is done to counter portrayals in some media that it is good to be bad. Education is the key.
One cannot expect law enforcement officials or the criminal justice system to succeed in the fight against organized crime without the support of society at large. More must be done to generate awareness of the economic and social impact of drug trafficking in Canada and abroad. Active measures which involve the community at large must be developed.
Bill C-264 speaks to an inconsistency in our approach to drug abuse. We prohibit the trafficking in or possession of illicit drugs, yet do nothing to prevent the commercial sale of paraphernalia which have no other use than to facilitate the consumption and use of such substances. To the average man or woman on the street, this is incomprehensible and I suspect that there is a great deal of support for the thrust for Bill C-264.
However, I have a major concern on which I would like to briefly touch. I am worried about that part of the proposed amendment to the Criminal Code which would have the effect of imposing a form of censorship over what Canadians are permitted to read. Hon. Members will note that the Bill makes no attempt to control any printed matter other than those few publications which specialize in the promotion of the consumption of illicit drugs. I am concerned that this legislation might be attacked under the provisions of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms which protect the freedom of expression and the freedom of communication of the press and other media.
Would the courts accept that there has been a need demonstrated for the introduction of such a measure? There are other publications disseminating information which, it could be argued, have no legitimate purpose in being distributed. Here I would refer the House to the report of the Senate Special Committee on Terrorism and the Public Safety which specifically addressed the topic of so-called mayhem manuals.
The committee recommended that the Government look at ways to prescribe the importation, production, distribution or sale of manuals which had as their dominant primary characteristic the description of how to fabricate weapons or bombs, or the description of tactics that could be of practical assistance in mounting terrorist attacks.
I believe a parallel may be drawn between these two types of publications, mayhem manuals on the one hand and literature for illicit drug use on the other. Neither serve any positive social purpose nor contribute to the good of Canadian society. Both are examples of specialized publications which reflect the views and interests of an extremely small segment of society. They are, however, instrumental in the dissemination of a set of values which are inconsistent with those held by the majority of Canadians. Both mayhem manuals and literature for illicit drug use are, in my submission, areas where the

March 11, 1988
Illicit Drugs Promotion
courts may support an exception to the protection of the fundamental freedoms listed in Section 2 of the Charter.
I have one final concern which also results from the Charter. The publishers of these specialized publications may point to their colleagues who communicate such information through other means and claim that they are being discriminated against. Would it not be wiser to expand the ambit of the proposed amendment to the Criminal Code to bring other forms of communication within its control?
In closing, I would invite Hon. Members to consider all aspects of this proposed legislation and not to dismiss it lightly. Fundamentally, what is proposed in Bill C-264 is sound and generally consistent with other legislation in this area. I salute the Hon. Member for Mississauga North for bringing this Bill forward. However, the working group established by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) to review the issue of drug paraphernalia will report within the year. I, therefore, recommend that the study of Bill C-264 be deferred until the conclusions of that report are known.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to enter this debate and offer some observations on the topic. For a period of time, mainly from 1969 to 1975, I worked with a youth agency in Vancouver where we very often dealt with young people who had overdosed on drugs, young people who had taken LSD and were on bummers, so to speak. I speak with a certain amount of knowledge as to the usage of illicit drugs, particularly in Vancouver during that period of the latter 1960s and the early 1970s.
I would like to say at the outset that the Private Members' Bill offered to us today really will not be very effective. You just do not deal with that problem by outlawing head shops, Mr. Speaker. It might satisfy some cravings of Hon. Members that they have struck a blow for righteousness and goodness, but I am afraid that is all it will do.
First, let us talk about head shops. Generally there are different types of cigarette paper. Does that mean you will outlaw all cigarette paper? That would be quite difficult. Does it mean that tobacconists will not be able to sell cigarette paper? That would be a little difficult. I hear an Hon. Member suggest that is a different thing. It really is not different. Essentially you can use these cigarette papers to roll a joint, a marijuana cigarette or a tobacco cigarette. To outlaw cigarette papers per se I do not think will accomplish very much. You can outlaw some of the other paraphernalia. Some of the other paraphernalia would be what is called "roach holders". For heaven's sake, Mr. Speaker, bobby pins can be used as roach holders. Will you outlaw bobby pins? Of course not, that is ridiculous. What about pipes? Some of these are what is called hookah pipes. Generally you find these in the Middle Eastern countries. They can be used either to smoke marijuana, hashish or tobacco. Will you outlaw them? Again, that is quite a different call to make. By outlawing pipes that can be used
for the smoking or inhaling of illegal substances, at the same time you will be prohibiting the smoking of legal substances. That does not make much sense either.
I suppose we now come to things that would be sold like posters and magazines that would extol the use of marijuana and other illicit substances. I might say that I have never seen a publication that encourages the use of what I would call the real dangerous drugs, namely, heroin, the hard drugs, the drugs that are addictive. I would say in my experience that marijuana, hashish and even mushrooms and LSD, from what I observed in the young people with whom I was dealing in Vancouver, are not really addictive. You can make a claim that they are psychologically addictive. Certainly I have known many young people who have used these substances on quite a regular basis, but you cannot describe them as being physically addictive as heroin would be, or, for that matter, alcohol or tobacco. In fact, from dealing with people who have gone through drug treatment programs, having been addicted to heroin, they tell me that they find it more difficult to quit smoking than to break the heroin habit. As I mentioned before, I have never seen a publication that extols the use or encourages the reader to use such hard drugs as heroin.
Are we going to outlaw these publications? The way the Bill is drafted, it is so open that major pieces of literature would also have to be outlawed. For instance, the Kubla Khan, A Vision in a Dream by Samuel Taylor Coleridge, Ulalume by Edgar Allen Poe, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes by Sir Arthur Conan Doyle, Alice in Wonderland by Lewis Carroll, Tropic of Capricorn by Henry Miller, Naked Lunch by William S. Burroughs, On the Road by Jack Kerouac, Howl and Other Poems by Allen Ginsburg, Beneath the Underdog by Charles Mingus and The Collected Works of Billy the Kid by Michael Ondaatje, winner of the Governor General's Award for poetry in 1971. Those are some of the publications that would conceivably fall under the ban proposed in this Private Members' Bill.
I do not understand why the drafter of the Bill, if he is concerned about magazines and pieces of literature that perhaps put into a positive light the taking of such illicit substances as marijuana and hashish, would stop at the printed word. Certainly popular music today, and has I would say for the last decade or decade and a half, has positive suggestions. There are several pieces by The Beatles that would also surely be banned if you used the same criteria that is being used in this Bill today.
Do well-intentioned Hon. Members, by outlawing and bringing the law to bear on businesses like head shops feel that they are doing something to deal with the drug problem? I would suggest that that is really not the case. They are really not dealing with the problem. It will not make any difference whatsoever if there are no so-called head shops around.

There is a drug problem that exists in society. Most of the problem has to do with hard drugs and with alcohol. Those two cause the most serious drug problems in society.
We all know about alcohol. We know of the untold deaths that occur on the highways because of drinking and driving. We know of marriage breakups that occur because of alcoholism within families. We know of the loss of jobs and economic security, again caused by alcoholism.
I would say that alcoholism is the most serious drug problem that exists in our society today. The second most serious problem is caused by heroin and morphine, two variations of the same drug, one being harder and having a different chemical consistency. In essence, they are both pain killers.
Heroin definitely causes serious social concerns. The funny thing is that part of the reason for heroin being a problem to society is that it is illegal. Mr. Speaker, unlike my colleague from the New Democratic Party who spoke before me, I do not think that my colleague from Mississauga North (Mr. Horner) introduced this Bill because he felt a wave of puritanism and wanted to express his opposition to a softening of social standards. On the contrary, I think he is a very responsible man who has seen the ravages caused by drugs among young people and who is looking for a solution to that problem.
This bill to amend the Criminal Code may not be the ideal or the only way to go about it, but I do not question in any way the sincerity of my colleague from Mississauga North when he approaches the problem by suggesting we must do something now.
Illicit Drugs Promotion
I know full well the ravages caused by drugs. I represent, Mr. Speaker, a constituency where 45 per cent of the urban population is under 35. About two years ago, I had to work with Gatineau policemen, particularly with police chief Joel Cheruet, to try and make illegal the setting up of arcades and pinball machines near elementary schools in the city of Gatineau. Because unfortunately in those arcades could be found not only pinball machines but also drug traffickers who took advantage of the tender age of those schoolchildren to get them addicted. As a result of their addiction, those children began to steal from automatic vending machines, in churches and also from older citizens coming back from senior citizens' clubs. They stole coins, mostly quarters from them to play those pinball machines in the arcades and to purchase drugs. It was noted that a gang of young schoolchildren were involved in drugs due to the proximity of those arcades where traffickers would be waiting for them.
Now this is a serious question. We found it difficult to convince civic authorities that such arcades near schools should be banned. They referred to business rights, to what my NDP colleague said a while ago about privacy and they told us that we should not be too coercive. Our efforts to protect those defenceless young people were thus undermined.
Faced with such a problem we should refrain from saying: "Oh dear, our community should not become puritan as a result of such problem." This is not the case. Indeed, we have a very serious problem.
I am also aware of the devastation caused by drugs because in my constituency there is an organization called Le bon samaritain led by Carole Dagenais, Carole Mongeon and Robert Gervais from the CIP and many others who are very devoted individuals. Those I know are working with former drug addicts. Whenever I visit "Le bon samaritain", I notice that the average age is very low. Therefore, it is a problem I am very familiar with.
I suggest it is our duty, as citizens, elected representatives and leaders of the community, not to discourage people like my friend the Hon. Member for Mississauga North when they suggest ways and means to try and stop drug trafficking. Rather than amending the Criminal Code, we could emphasize and enhance a number of Criminal Code provisions. I refer for instance to Section 422 of the Code which states:
422. Except where otherwise expressly provided by law, the following provisions apply in respect of persons who counsel other persons to commit offences, namely,
(a)	every one who counsels another person to commit an indictable offence is, if the offence is not committed, guilty of an indictable offence and is liable to the same punishment to which a person who attempts to commit that offence is liable; and
(b)	every one who counsels another person to commit an offence punishable on summary conviction is, if the offence is not committed, guilty of an offence punishable on summary conviction.
I was quoting from 1953-54, Chap. 51, Sec. 407; 1985, Chap. 19, Sec. 61.

March 11, 1988
Illicit Drugs Promotion
So, Section 22 of the Criminal Code defines a "counsellor" as a person who counsels or procures another person to be a party to an offense. Jurisprudence has it that, in order to obtain a conviction, it is not necessary to prove that the other person has committed the offense which was counselled to him or her by the accused. Simple counselling is enough for an offense. So we could use this section.
It would be difficult to find a basic difference between the action the people doing that kind of counselling are accused of and the behaviour of the people involved in the sale of illicit drug paraphernalia. Under the Criminal Code, it is clear that offering the devices and kits freely available in the so-called "head shops" to make the use and, therefore, possession of illicit drugs more attractive, make any person, especially the owners and employees of the shops, liable to criminal pursuit for having counseled persons into committing an offense.
1 hope that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) will consider using Section 422 of the Criminal Code as a means to solve the problem resulting from the possession and sale of illicit drug paraphernalia in this country.
Accordingly, Mr. Speaker, if this Bill was voted on and deferred to a legislative committee, we could deal with the measures suggested by my colleague the Hon. Member for Mississauga North (Mr. Horner) for the purpose of improving it and dealing then with the use of Section 422 or other ways to proceed. However, Mr. Speaker, I object to people imputing motives on someone who wishes to deal with the difficult drug addiction problem, especially when young people are involved. I would like to suggest to the Hon. Member for Regina East (Mr. de Jong) that instead of taking offense for a wording that might differ from his way of life or his ideas, he participates in a constructive way to this debate in order that we find, and this very rapidly, the best possible solution to this terrible problem. I wish as well to encourage my colleagues in the House to actively participate in crime prevention movements that are being launched here and there in Canada, because parents of young people already hooked are often those who assume the whole task.
I believe those fortunate enough to have children who escaped this drug addiction calamity should get very personally involved with these prevention groups, because they are the ones who could bring with a clear mind the right answers, whereas parents of children who were once or still are drug addicts are sometimes so emotionally disturbed by their family problem that they fail to calmly consider the issue.
I thank you, Mr. Speaker, for having listened to me with much attention and 1 am sure that my colleagues will have a second thought before casting aspersions on a person who only wishes to resolve such a problem.
