speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to comment on that important question. The Hon. Member for Mississauga North (Mr. Horner) has introduced a legislation amending the Criminal
Code to prohibit the sale of drug paraphernalia. As we all know, while narcotics and some other drugs are actually prohibited, it is still possible and easy to find litterature promoting such drug use as well as drug paraphernalia and kits in shops specializing in the sale of such paraphernalia.
You will remember, Mr. Speaker, that the Government has announced last May its national Strategy against drug use thus manifesting its firm intention of finding solutions to the problem of drug abuse. The matter of drug paraphernalia is directly related to the problem of drug abuse.
As you will surely know, several states have passed legislations to eliminate the sale of drug paraphernalia. I would like to take a few moments to trace the history of the problem of drug parahernalia South of our frontier.
Early in the 1960's, most Americans had almost never experimented with drugs, except naturally for alcool, tobacco and coffee. It is through newspapers, novels and movies that people have learned about the way of life of the drug addicts. It was among the poor, mainly the black, the Spanish immigrants and the native that illicit drug use was more prevalent. In their mind, the people associated drug use with criminals and other marginal sub-cultures such as the beatnicks among whom some of the greatest poets, artists and musicians of their generation are found. The average American did not have much to go with drugs but they were omnipresent in the dregs of society as well as among the anti-establishment intelligentsia.
As the 1960's went by, drug abuse skyrocketed. Thanks to progress made in medicine and in pharmacology the number of available drugs increased considerably. Vitamins began to be used in millions of homes. Large immunization campaigns were carried out. Millions of people were prescribed tranquilizers for the relief of stress symptoms.
The introduction of oral contraceptives has set in motion a sexual revolution and created a direct association between pills and pleasure. Other factors, such as social unrest prevalent in those times, have contributed to an increase in drug abuse behaviour. Arts and cinema became psychedelic; in Woodstock, the generation of the Sixties was celebrating its liberation with protest songs and acid rock.
Civil disobedience had become the accepted way of fighting against discrimination, encouraged by the State. The notion that governments could and should be opposed has contributed to the political anti-establishment activities which have marked the Vietnam War years. In the late Sixties and early Seventies, the morality of the governments and of the Establishment was questioned, and many people, mostly young people, were suspicious of the foreign racial and drugs policies of the United States. Even in the most respectable circles it was good to criticize government policy, and the attitude towards drugs was the most permissive ever seen. Pressure groups were set up to promote the reform of drug legislation and some States went even as far as to decriminalize marijuana. In many other States, sentences imposed for minor drug
March II, 1988

offences became much lighter in most if not all cases. In that context, it is impossible to ascertain if the increase in drug abuse resulted from a temporary mental aberration or rather from the cohesion of a sub-culture. But repression of drug abuse, so dearly won during the first half of the century, was wiped out within a decade. The most widespread drugs were marijuana, pharmaceutical products, hallucinogens and, to a certain extent, cocain and opiates.
On the list of articles useful or necessary for drug use, we find pipes, water pipes, cigarette papers, tweezers, mirrors, razor blades and a whole range of accessories for illicit preparation, conservation and consumption of illegal drugs.
Those accessories, although they were not widely available, appeared in the sixties in headshops and record stores. Their growing popularity brought about an increase in the number of stores where they were available. The marketing and distribution became more and more sophisticated. In 1974, the magazine High Times was published for the first time, 20,000 copies being printed; it was an immediate hit. High Times publishes reports and editorials pushing for recreational use of drugs while at the same time providing the manufacturers of thoses accessories with a medium to advertise their products.
Opposition against the instrument industry first came from parents, church leaders, and government authorities. In the early days the opposition was weak and disorganized. The first organized group that challenged the drug device makers was established in 1977 in the American state of Georgia. Its members maintained that the whole industry was violating the government's drug control policies and that shops gave youngsters the impression that drugs were socially acceptable. Similar groups were set up in other parts of the country and brought pressure to bear on local governments so they would issue regulations outlawing the sale of drug paraphernalia.
Between 1977 and 1979 a number of states and municipalities passed legislation to prohibit possession and distribution of such devices. Those first laws were all declared unconstitutional. In May, 1979, the White House requested that the Department of Justice's Drug Enforcement Agency attempt to develop a constitutionally permissible approach to the control of paraphernalia.
The DEA's response to the White House request was to develop a model drug paraphernalia Act. Hearings were held before the House Select Committee on Narcotics and Drug Abuse control in November, 1979, to review the model Act. The committee concluded its review by finding that the paraphernalia industry contributed to the flagrant and harmful use of drugs and found that the model Act was necessary to eradicate the paraphernalia industry.
I would like to go over some of the basic provisions of the American model Act.
First, it provides a comprehensive definition of the term "drug paraphernalia" with specific descriptions of the most common forms of paraphernalia.
Illicit Drugs Promotion
It lists the factors which must be taken into account to determine whether an item is covered by this definition.
It makes it an offense to manufacture, advertise, deliver or use drug paraphernalia.
It makes it a special offense to deliver drug paraphernalia to anyone under 18 years of age.
It precisely defines outlawed acts in the manufacture, advertising, delivery and use of drug paraphernalia and specifies the culpable intent necessary to commit the offense.
It provides for seizure and confiscation of drug paraphernalia.
To date, some 40 American states have adopted the uniform legislation proposed to control drug paraphernalia.
In my opinion, the problem of drug abuse and drug paraphernalia is more serious in the United States than in Canada. We can only approve any initiative which might help to put an end to the social calamity which drug use has now become. The purpose of the Bill introduced by the Hon. Member is quite laudable, but I do not believe that the means suggested by the Hon. Member are appropriate to meet this purpose. In any case, the Department of Justice has undertaken a review of this whole issue, and during this process, it will consult those concerned and professional groups. It should be able to publish its conclusions later this year. I therefore believe, Mr. Speaker, that the debate should be postponed until the findings of this study have been published.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   CRIMINAL CODE MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am most pleased to participate in this debate. While we certainly endorse the comments that have been made by a number of speakers this afternoon, we would like to point out that Bill C-264 is in fact a follow-through on what has already been proposed by a standing committee of the House of Commons. More specifically, Mr. Speaker, you will recall that last year the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) deemed that because there was a drug epidemic in the United States, there was also a drug epidemic in Canada. As a result of that statement, there was a study launched by the Standing Committee on National Health and Welfare which examined the whole range of licit and illicit drugs in Canada.
One of the areas which that committee studied was head shops and the paraphernalia sold in head shops. The committee made a number of very salient and proper recommendations in that regard. That report was entitled "Booze, Pills & Dope; Reducing Substance Abuse in Canada" and was tabled

March 11, 1988
Illicit Drugs Promotion
here in the House of Commons some months ago. Yet, we have heard absolutely nothing from the Government.
It is all well and good for us to stand up and say "Let's support this wonderful Private Member's Bill". With respect, Mr. Speaker, it is motherhood. Of course no one in their right mind is going to stand up and say that we should support the sale of illegal drug paraphernalia in Canada. Of course we should be acting.
However, I must ask the Government today why it is leaving the job up to Private Members in the form of Private Members' Bills and why it has refused to respond to the Standing Committee on National Health and Welfare when in September, 1986, I believe, the Prime Minister said that there was a drug epidemic. He has had a report on the matter sitting on the desk of the Government for a number of months and there has been no response.
Therefore, can we stop hiding behind Private Members' Bills and the very good intentions of Members of Parliament on all sides of the House and start doing something, start showing some leadership? Private Members' Bills in this House will be debated. We will all have a chance to put our thoughts on the record and send our messages to our constituents so that they will know that we are speaking out on the important issues. However, Private Members' Bills seldom become the law of the land.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) has had in his possession a series of recommendations which specifically address the problem of head shops in Canada and he has chosen to ignore them. Why do we not cut out this hypocrisy?
According to Standing Order 96(2) the the study "Booze, Pills & Dope; Reducing Substance Abuse in Canada" was reported to the House of Commons and we are still waiting for the reply of the Government. There were a number of government Members on this committee. The Member for Oxford (Mr. Halliday) was the chairman of the committee and the Member for Ottawa-Carleton (Mr. Turner) was the vicechairman. The Members for York Scarborough (Mr. McCros-san), Dauphin-Swan River (Mr. White), and Nipissing (Mr. Mantha) were members of the committee as well as myself and the Member for Saint-Maurice (Mr. Grondin). A lot of Members worked on this report and came up with some extremely good recommendations, one of which specifically dealt with the question of drug paraphernalia and nothing has been done.
